speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JUDGMENT OF SUPREME COURT ON QUESTION SUBMITTED
speechtext: I have been informed that the judgment of the supreme court was delivered to-day, and their judgment is that under the British North America Act women are not eligible for appointment to the senate. I understand that the basis for the judgment is that the act must be interpreted in the meaning it had when it was adopted in 1867, and that at that time (the expression " fit and qualified persons " as it appears in the act could not apply to women as they were then disqualified for appointment to public offices. The judgment was unanimous. In view of this judgment, and in view of the faict that women in this country now have an equal franchise with men, and in view of the further fact that one of the seats in this house is occupied by a woman, the government have decided that they should have the equal right to sit in the other Chamber, and means will be taken to secure an amendment to the British North America Act in that respect.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 218 to amend the Federal District Commission Act, 1927.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this
bill is to make provision for certain capital expenditures by the federal district commission to carry out a plan of improvement and
2312	[DOT] COMMONS
Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
beautification in the centre of Ottawa as the capital of Canada, also to extend the period of time of the annual appropriation to be made to the commission for the purpose of maintaining improvements which have already been made. The act proposes an immediate appropriation of $3,000,000 as an amount to serve for capital expenditure in connection with improvements which the commission has in contemplation. Provision is made whereby this amount may be advanced to the commission direct by the Minister of Finance and made a charge upon the consolidated revenue, or advanced upon the issue of securities by the commission, these to extend over a period of thirty years. The principal and interest of such securities are to be guaranteed by the Department of Finance and to be redeemed by a sinking fund to be maintained by the department for that purpose. The annual appropriation for purposes of maintenance is being reduced from $250,000 per annum at which it now stands to $200,000 per annum.
That the bill is being introduced at the present time is due to the fact that last fall the government was advised by the federal district commission and by the city council that the owners of the Russell house property were contemplating the immediate demolition of that property and had applied to the city for the right to erect a new modem hotel on the site. The federal commission pointed out that if that step were taken at the present time it would interfere with what they believed was a development which should be made and made speedily within the central part of the city; and the city council pointed out that unless the government could give some immediate reason why a permit should not be granted to the hotel authorities to go on with the erection of the new hotel, the board of control would be obliged to give the permit for that purpose.
I might say that at the time the government was informed of this proposal on the part of the Russell house owners the work of demolishing the old property had already commenced, and the government was given to understand that plans had been called for and were being prepared for the new hotel which was about to be erected. It was apparent that either a decision had to be reached immediately or in the event of a postponement, and the property being subsequently acquired, that a very much greater outlay would be necessary to indemnify the owners against expenditures which they might be put to in the interval of time between that at which the government might authorize the immediate expropriation of the property and

the time at which parliament might be in a position to grant authority for the expropriation.
In the circumstances, and more particularly because of other circumstances which I shall mention, it seemed to the administration advisable to give to the federal district commission the authority to expropriate immediately the properties in question. The further reasons were the following: to have allowed the owners of the hotel to erect a modern hotel on the old site, having regard to improvements that the government had already made and improvements that were in immediate contemplation, became the equivalent of presenting the finest site in the capital of Canada, to a company which was proposing to build a hotel in no way equal to the Chateau Laurier, but one that While large and serviceable would not, it was thought, in any way approach in architectural beauty the other hotel which is in the near vicinity of the parliament buildings. It would have meanit that going from parliament hill into the heart of the city the new hotel would be the structure immediately f acing all the visitors to parliament hill. It would have meant further that so far as the company was concerned they would have had as a frontage for their hotel the advantage of the expropriation that had already been made between Wellington street and Sparks street west of Elgin street and this side of the post office and an. immediate view of the houses of parliament. They would have had at one side all the improvement which is being made o*n the driveway between the canal and the present Russell house property, and they would virtually be given by the country this exceptional environment, which the government felt ought really to belong to the country as a whole. In the circumstances, conferences were held with the federal district commission and with the members of the board of control and the city council as to whether in some way an arrangement for joint action could not be made between the city and the commission, in the event of the government undertaking to alltow tihe expropriation of the Russell house properties. It Was discovered, after some little conference, that the city was prepared to cooperate with the federal district commission to make the central part of the city all that the members of this house and the citizens of Canada generally could wish the centre of the capital of the Dominion to be.
In order that I may bring to the minds of the members of the house the nature of the proposed improvements and just what was before us as we were considering the matter, I would recall that the government of Canada

Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
owns practically all the land that is on the south shore of the Ottawa river from the old Perley home on the west to beyond the archives building on the east. The parliament buildings stand practically in the centre of that stretch. Opposite the parliament buildings is the property on which the Chateau Laurier is at present situated with Major Hill park immediately behind it, and the Daly building which is property the government of Canada has acquired. That means that a'lll the land which lies immediately to the south of government property along Wellington street between the east block and the Chateau Laurier, and whiioh is intersected by the Rideau canal, is pretty much in t'he centre of property now owned by the government. It is also in the centre of the city, and for the most part to all intents and purposes already a large park area. There are still some buildings on parts of it, but at comparatively little cost to-day the whole can be made quickily and readily into a great central park, facing, as I have said, on property already owned by the government.
There is the open space with which hon. members are familiar, between Wellington and Sparks streets and between Elgin street and the post office, and which has been expropriated. From there to the station except for the city post office it is all open space. The Rideau canal is government property and the property to the right of it also owned by the government, constitutes, at the present time, a driveway in the course of improvement. A large area has been opened up by the commission on the property formerly occupied by the old Dey's rink which fronts on Laurier avenue. Beyond Laurier avenue there is Cartier square which is already a park owned by the Dominion and beyond Cartier square are the grounds of the collegiate institute, the normal school and the model school, all of which are government-owned properties. Those latter properties are owned by the provincial government. Hon. members will therefore see that with the exception of the few buildings that front west on Elgin street and a few buildings fronting on Nicholas street on the far side of the canal which are of an antiquated character, omitting a few principal structures that face on Rideau street beyond the railway station, all the area to the north and south lying between the Ottawa river and Lisgar street and to the east and west between Elgin street and Nicholas street is to-day virtually one large park area.
The commission pointed out to the government that without any very great expenditure, having regard to the significance of the
properties to be acquired, this vast area might be made into a park in the very centre of the capital of Canada. As I have said, the government felt that to allow the most important part of that property to remain in the hands of private owners and be used for a public hotel would, in the light of the circumstances I have mentioned, livery short-sighted and would show a distinct lack of vision on the part of the administration in regard to the future development of the capital of our country. To allow members to see the scheme of development which is proposed I have had a plan prepared by the commission. If I could have copies of these plans distributed, hon. members would be in a position to follow more easily what is proposed with respect to the development that is contemplated.
As bon. members we'll know, the business centre of the city so far as traffic is concerned has come more and more to be that particular part of Ottawa lying between Elgin street on the one side and the central station on the other. It is also the part that is for the most part used as an approach to and as an egress from parliament hill1. Although our grounds of parliament have a main entrance, it is not used to anything like the same extent as the entrance at the head of Elgin street. That means that traffic more and more is concentrated at the very doors of parliament, and already it is evident, I think, to all who have given any thought to the question, that there is need for a better regulation and distribution of traffic in the immediate vicinity of these houses of parliament. The commission therefore proposes as a central feature of the development, if parliament appropriates the money for the purpose, to make a large circular space around which the traffic of the city will have to move in one direction in the area through which Sparks street runs at the present time and which is bounded on the south by the present Ruase'll house and on the north by the square that has already been expropriated. The idea would be to have something corresponding to what in the city of London, England, one sees at Piccadilly circus or Oxford oircus whereby in the centre of the city the traffic would be obliged to move one way around the sides olf a circle and into which particular area the different streets would run. That centre would be virtually the heart of the .capital. In all probability, when the erection of the national war memorial is further under consideration it will be thought advisable that the memorial should 'be placed in the centre of that circle.

May I add that at the present time, as hon. members know, there is no single point at which the parliament buildings in their entirety can be viewed from any distance? Beautiful as they are, prominently as they are placed on this hill, there is not in Ottawa any point at which, when one gets beyond Wellington street, these buildings -can be viewed as a whole. If the park project which is proposed is carried through, there will be given from the greater part of the park a commanding view of the parliament buildings. Indeed it is proposed -that there should be constructed from the Laurier avenue bridge a driveway which will run- diagonally through the heart of the park and which will, coming up to the approach at Elgin street entrance, afford to anyone approaching the parliament buildings a complete view of their imposing front. In other words, a visitor to the city standing on Laurier aven-ue bridge, situated as it is at present, would get from that point an unobstructed view of the main entrances of the houses of parliament. The memorial tower in the centre would be practically in the centre of that view and the avenue that would approach the building would be the main avenue to the houses of parliament. All of us, I think, regret only too sincerely that when the buildings were placed where they are, some system of city or town planning was not followed whereby there would have been an adequate and dignified approach to the houses of parliament. But if we feel the lack of that approach to-day; if we feel there has been an omission in that particular in the past, I am inclined to believe that those who come after us will realize the omission even more than we do, an-d will regard us as having been remiss if, seeing the situation as we now see it, we do not endeavour -to improve and rectify it.
If hon. members will look at the plan which the federal district commission have drafted of what they have proposed, they will see that it virtually corresponds with what I have in this brief way sought to outline. Having regard to the properties that lie on the east side of the canal and to the west of Nicholas street, may I say further that for the most part they are already owned by either the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or the Canadian National Railways? I have personally had talks with Mr. Beatty, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and with Sir Henry Thornton, of the Canadian National Railways, and asked if their companies would be prepared to co-operate with the city and with the commission in improving that particular area in so far as their interest in it is concerned, and I have their assurances that

they will be only too happy to further to whatever extent may be necessary so far as their companies are concerned the work of the improvement and beautification of the heart of the capital of Canada.
May I say that the government naturally was hesitant about adopting this proposal before having an opportunity of submitting the project in its entirety to parliament, but as I have just explained, it was a matter of then deciding or of necessitating later on through delay a very much larger outlay. Moreover, so far as the decision itself is concerned, and that is what I think bears immediately on our consideration of the matter here, it would appear to be a case of deciding now or never whether these particular properties shall be obtained. Naturally a time comes in the development of every city where new buildings take the place of old ones, and unless the government takes steps immediately to acquire the properties I have mentioned, it is altogether probable that new structures of a very costly character will be erected, and that any future government will find it -all but impossible to proceed with a development of the kind.
Had the government been obliged to trust solely to its own judgment in this matter, possibly the decision would have been as it is, but fortunately the government had before it the expressions of view and opinion of hon. members of this house during the last session when the amendment was brought in to the Ottawa Improvement Commission Act, and the name of the commission was changed to that of its present designation as the federal district commission. At that time several hon. members of the house spoke with reference to the appropriation which the government was then asking from parliament, and I think almost without exception-there was exception taken on the part of one or two-but almost without exception the expression of view as given from all parts of the house was that the government's request for the purpose for which the appropriation was intended was far too modest. The then leader of the opposition, the hon. Mr. Guthrie, member for South Wellington, speaking for himself and I judged for his friends in his party, said that he thought the appropriation w-e had asked for should be several times what it was, and he very wisely, I think, drew attention to the importance of making changes without loss of time and of seeking to make Ottawa, as it should be, worthy in all respects as the capital of the Dominion. My hon. friend the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was in the house at the time and participated in the debate, and if not in express terms, was, I

Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
think on the whole most sympathetic with the views of the then leader of the opposition. My hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) also spoke and expressed approval of what the government was then doing and his belief, I think, that for the capital we could not go too far in planning further developments along right lines. From among the ranks of hon. gentlemen apposite, the hon. member forOarleton (Mr. Garland) also spoke, strongly advocating the appropriation of a much larger sum. Then my friend the leader of the Progressives mentioned, if I recollect aright, or if he himsellf personally did not, some of bis following did express their approval of the course the government was then taking, and I know that one hon. member in particular, the hon. member for Maideod (Mr. Coote), said that he thought there had been great neglect in the approaches to the parliament buildings, and he advocated steps being taken in the near future which would improve the approaches to parliament hill. In these circumstances I think I am correct in Saying that the government was justified at least in feeling that when it came to parliament with the present proposal, hon. members, in. view of what had been said, as well as what was left unsaid, would view with approval the step which is now being taken.
May I add that there are other reasons why I believe the house would be justified in giving its approval to the present bill? The proposal has now been before the country for some little time, and the press in all parts of the country has made observations with respect to it. I have yet to discover from any journal of importance a criticism of what is being proposed. Throughout the Dominion there is a feeling that the capital of the country should be made worthy not only of its present; but of its future. If this is to be done, Something along the lines now being proposed is necessary.
We had in Ottawa last fall an important conference of the premiers of the several provinces with members of the federal government. The subject of the improvement of the capital along the lines indicated was not taken up as a matter of formal discussion at any meeting of the conference, but personally I had a word with the premiers of the provinces as to their opinion, from the point of view of their respective provinces, of what the Dominion was about to undertake in the matter of the improvement of the capital. I do not think that I am' misrepresenting any of them when I say that I gathered from their expressions of opinion very hearty approval of a proposal such as is now being presented to the house.
May I add in particular one further justification for the step which the government is now proposing? In 1913, before the war, the government of Sir Robert Borden appointed a commission known as the "federal plan commission on a general plan for the cities of Ottawa and Hull." The commission was appointed in September, 1913, and its members were:
His Worship, the mayor of Ottawa.
His Worship, the mayor of Hull.
Sir Alexandre Lacoste, K.C., of the city of Montreal.
Herbert S. Holt, Esq., of the city of Montreal.
Frank Darling, Esq., of the city of Toronto.
R. Home Smith, Esq., of the city of Toronto.
The order in council appointing the commission charged it with the duty of-
-taking all necessary steps to draw up and perfect a comprehensive scheme or plan looking to the future growth and development of the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull, and their environs, and particularly providing for the location, laying out and beautification of parks and connecting boulevards, the location and architectural character of public buildings, and adequate and convenient arrangements for traffic and transportation within the area in question.
The commission made its report two years later, in 1915, and I have a copy of that report in my hand. The report is a most valuable one, and undoubtedly it was prepared by the then government for the very purpose which we are now seeking to further in bringing before the house the proposal I am submitting in this bill. Without question the recommendations of the commission would, in part at least, have been acted upon long before this had the war not intervened, and may I say that the proposal now being made parallels in many respects a central feature of the proposals made by the commission appointed by Sir Robert Borden at that time. These gentlemen were of the view that it was all-important that the central part of the city should be reserved as an open space, and that the buildings surrounding it should be of a character to lend dignity and harmony to other important buildings in the capital.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I say a word with respect to the obligation of parliament towards Ottawa as the capital city of the Dominion. I know it will be said by some hon. gentlemen that the government is doing a great deal for this city. We must however be careful to distinguish between what the government is doing for Ottawa as a city, and what the government is doing for Ottawa as the capital of this Dominion. It is impossible for any municipality to undertake the sort of

planning and development required for the capital of a country. If it is to have a capital, a country must expect to incur obligations and expenditures incidental to its development, whether that capital be in some newly-acquired and undeveloped area, as is the case to-day with respect to the Australian capital about to be developed, or in some existing municipality. No municipality could undertake on purely municipal lines the kind of development which would be necessary to make its city a capital worthy of the country. And so I ask hon. members in considering what the government is proposing to do so from the point of view of the obligation of this parliament to the capital of Canada.
In connection with the Choice of a capital, may I remind hon. members that Ottawa was not chosen originally as the capital of this great Dominion. In 1858, before confederation, this city was chosen as the capital of the two provinces that were united under the Act of Union. It was not until after practical developments had taken place on parliament hill, it was not until after the corner stone of the parliament buildings had been laid and their erection completed-all of which was done in relation to one province as it then existed-that the fathers of confederation, seeing the possibilities of Ottawa as the future capital of the Dominion, decided to have it become the national capital. Up to that time Ottawa had been a community that had but recently emerged from the backwoods. It was for the most part concerned with lumbering operations and manufacturing incidental thereto. Transportation also incidental to those developments had taken shape in different directions, but there was no general plan of the city. It had never been thought of as a capital; it was simply, as I have said, a community that had emerged out of the primitive forest and had taken shape from day to day pretty much as industrial development progressed. Then came confederation, and it was decided to make Ottawa the capital of what at the time was a dominion of but four provinces.
What I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members is this. From that stage the city continued practically as it then was, until the time when the Ottawa improvement commission was organized, and it is owing largely to this fact that to-day we find no adequate approaches to parliament hill or to the houses of parliament. I need not remind hon. members that it was not until 1905, when the prairie provinces came into confederation, that for the first time we had a Dominion extending from sea to sea, linking together

organized provinces in all parts of Canada. That was only twenty-three years ago. So that when in relation to its future we speak of Ottawa as the capital of this Dominion, we have to keep in mind that this capital to-day, as representative of the whole of Canada, is a capital that speaks for but twenty-three years' growth of the Dominion constitutionally organized as it is to-day.
That being the case, what is going to be the position of Ottawa in the next twenty-three years, in the next fifty years, in the next one hundred years to. say nothing of a much longer period? It is our duty to consider that situation, and I submit that if hon. members will consider the future development of the capital from that point of view they will see the wisdom of not losing further time in planning for its proper development. Already the evidences of the lack of foresight are only too manifest. Take the main approach to the front entrance of these buildings already referred to, Metcalfe street. It ought to be a magnificent boulevard and a grand approach to these houses of parliament, but as viewed from the main entrance it is pretty much in the nature of a country lane; it is not very much larger. There is practically no approach to parliament hill from Metcalfe street at the present time. The same is true of O'Connor street at the western end of the grounds; and the same was true of Elgin street until the changes made last year had dome into 'being. These effects of the lack of foresight on the part of those who had to do with the previous development should cause us to have regard for the rapid development that will take place in the near future. We have on the other hand, an example of what can 'be done by a little foresight. Fortunately the Ottawa improvement commission was created some years ago. The commission was granted a limited amount of money, but it has followed a course of development of the city in laying out parks and boulevards which has given to the capital a character of its own, in which not only those who come to attend parliament have a pride, but in which with pride the whole Dominion shares. Having before us, on the one hand, the evidences of neglect and their consequences, and on the other hand, the evidences of what can be done by a little careful planning, with regard to the future, I say we would indeed be remiss in our duty, if now, at a moment when the opportunity is so great and when the omission would be so serious, we did not take full account of the opportunity and make the most of it

Federal District*-Mr. Mackenzie King
In order to illustrate what I am seeking to bring home to hon. members, may I ask them to 'compare for a moment the capital of the Dominion with the respective capitals of the individual provinces, and see whether what the government is asking should be done for our national capital is in any sense extravagant in comparison with what the individual provinces have already done for their respective capitals. In the city of Toronto, the provincial buildings are located in Queen's park-«, magnificent setting, not as fine as that of parliament hill, but rendered much more beautiful and magnificent by the approach to it. If we had an avenue running up to parliament hill comparable to University avenue in Toronto, this city would take on an entirely different complexion. My view is that parliament would not only be justified in taking but really ought to take steps immediately to make an approach to the main entrance of the houses of parliament similar to that which has been made with respect to the legislative buildings in Toronto. I am not, however, going to advocate that at the moment. I simply say that it is ,a step which, if not taken to-day, will be taken by some future government and will then be taken at enormously greater cost than would be involved at the present time. Then take the city of Quebec. There again you have the legislative buildings beautifully situated in a large, open space, and surrounded by improvements on which there have been vast expenditures. But take the western provinces, the newer provinces that could least afford to make large outlays on their public buildings. Look at British Columbia; the legislative buildings in Victoria are situated in surroundings infinitely finer than those of parliament hill in their relationship to the city. Come to Alberta: the grounds surrounding the legislative buildings in the city of Edmonton are, if anything, finer than those of the capital of Canada. Take the city of Regina: at one time Regina was practically a rolling prairie waste, to-day the legislative buildings in that city are situated in the centre of a very lovely park, embracing many acres of beautifully cultivated grounds with an artificial lake and other attractions. The province of Saskatchewan has felt it could make towards the improvement and the dignifying of the capital of that province an expenditure many times greater, comparatively speaking, than what is now being suggested for the capital of the Dominion of Canada. In Manitoba the surroundings of the legislative buildings represent, again, on the part of the public authorities, a much greater regard for their immediate environment and for the appearance of the 56103-147i
city, as a provincial capital, than anything we have in this federal capital at the present time.
With regard to the other provinces, with their legislative buildings at Halifax, Nova Scotia, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, and Fredericton, New Brunswick, I cannot speak with equal knowledge, although I think that, having regard to the size and the needs of each of these provinces, the immediate environment of the legislative buildings in these maritime provinces represents more in the way of sacrifice on the part of the legislatures and of the people than anything which this Dominion has made towards the improvement of its capital.
I hope I have helped to bring home what I really feel we cannot emphasize too often, namely, the position of this city as the capital of the Dominion of Canada. Ottawa is the focal centre of the Dominion; it is the capital of a dominion which is rapidly growing and which is acknowledged as the first of the dominions of the British Empire. It is the heart of a nation that has grown great not only in its own affairs but in the affairs of the world at large, and the time has come when thought cannot be given too seriously to the future possibilities of this city as a capital city.
I have made comparisons with our own provinces. But there are other comparisons which perhaps should be made when one is discussing Ottawa as the capital of a nation. Take the capitals of other countries-and these, again, I mention more for the purpose of emphasizing the fact that a country is largely known among the nations of the world by its capital. Take the city of London, the capital of Great Britain. I need not emphasize what the city of London means to the world as the capital of Great Britain. But I should like to point out just what it has cost the city of London in some particulars to make a very few changes that have become necessary largely because London is the capital- changes which might have been made a short time ago at comparatively little cost. Within the last couple of years the city of London has been obliged to spend more than $125,000,000 in the purchase of land for the purpose of cutting two new streets through the city; and many other millions have also been spent in tearing down buildings for the construction of thoroughfares. At the time of the great fire in London, Sir Christopher Wren pleaded with the authorities of the day to widen one or two of the main thoroughfares of that city. That plea was met with the same kind of objection often encountered by measures of this character namely that
231S	COMMONS
Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
they do not bear all their fruit in the immediate present: it was contended that the expenditure was one that should not then be incurred. And it was not incurred. But to-day the citizens of London have had to pay on the widening of two streets alone- in addition to millions spent in tearing down different structures-the sum of $125,000,000 for the small additional leeway which has been thereby afforded.
I come now to Paris. In the eyes of the world Paris typifies France. What position did the French government take a few years ago with regard to their capital? Paris as a city had not been planned as the capital of France. The French authorities, realizing the importance of creating 'a dignified capital, had plans carefully studied, and an appropriation made for the improvement of the city. In 1853 the city of Paris spent $265,000,000 on Baron Haussmann's plans to open up the French capital to light and air and to create beautiful parks and boulevards. The sum of $265,000,000! Is there anyone who has visited Paris who does not feel that that investment, large as it was, has been a good one for the French people? Every visitor comes away feeling that Paris is one of the most beautiful capitals, if not the most beautiful, in the world. Indeed, one receives the impression that the French nation has had its character moulded and shaped to some considerable extent by the expression given to its capital city.
Then come to the United States. At the time Washington was decided upon as the capital of that republic, George Washington, in conference with Jefferson, the Secretary of State, foresaw that a great nation would arise upon this continent in the territory of the United States. Plans were made accordingly. Hon. members have heard of the work of L'Enfant who at that time, retained by Washington and the Secretary of State, laid out vast plans for the development of parks and driveways in what was to be the future capital of the United States. These plans were laughed at. They were declared to be ridiculous. Nevertheless they were accepted by the government, who retained the areas outlined for parks and driveways, with the result that the United States for over one hundred years has had secured to its capital many of its very beautiful parks and driveways. For an interval of years those plans fell into disuse, but a little later, at considerable expense, a commission for the beautification of Washington was appointed in order to see what further development might be carried out. That commission, including some of the great architects and sculptors of

the United States, having gone very thoroughly into the matter, ultimately came back to the plans of L'Enfant, declaring that there was nothing they could recommend which would constitute an improvement on the suggestions that had been made a century before. Washington is modeled on those plans, and if I may make a comparison in order to indicate in a degree the very little that we are proposing here compared to what is obviously a pressing need of Washington today-and a similar need will suggest itself in this country some day-I would direct the attention of hon. members to the development which is being prosecuted in the heart of Washington, the large Mall that connects the capitol with the residence of the president. There is in Washington a park area that stretches for two miles, the whole of it forming a central park in the heart of the capital of the United States. From that park centre there radiate various driveways which hellp to imipart to Washington the great icharm which it possesses as a capital.
We are asking parliament to vote a sum sufficient to enable us to create a small central park about one-tenth the size I have suggested -or rather, I should say, one-twenty-fifth of that size-in the heart of this Canadian capital. What is Washington spending today towards the upkeep of the United States capital? She is contributing, towards permanent improvements in parks, apart from all that has already been spent, an annual appropriation of $245,000 and a maintenance appropriation of $705,000, or a total of $951,-000-nearly a million dollars annually, just for maintenance and small improvements in the park areas which have already been developed. But in addition to that she is appropriating large sums of money for special improvements. One that is being developed at present is a bridge known as the Arlington memorial bridge, which is being constructed at a cost of $14,500,000. This is simply one approach to this park, or rather one connecting link between it and Arlington cemetery, which is being added as an additional feature of adornment to the capital of the United States. I believe it is correct to say that when one adds to the expenditures made on parks and driveways in Washington the expenditures which are made on public buildings, they total on an average for recent years about $9,000,000 a year. That is how Washington is being developed, and everyone knows that when the world speaks of Washington it gets a vision of the United States.
I shall not take up the time of the house by citing other examples beyond making mention of one which is related to another part of

Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
the British Empire. The Commonwealth of Australia found itself in a position not wholly dissimilar to that of Canada; the capital had been at Melbourne, which was not originally intended as a capital city. It was discovered amongst other things that it would mean an enormous cost properly to develop the heart of what was already a commercial city. At great expense and sacrifice the government decided to acquire an entirely new area and to make of the capital of Australia a model city. The property for the federal capital of Australia was purchased from the state of New South Wales and vested, in the commonwealth on January 1, 1910. The total area is about 900 square miles, or 576,000 acres. The land set aside for the capital site comprises twelve square miles, and 100,000 acres is set apart for public buildings, military colleges, reserves, parks and roads. During the fiscal year of 1925 the federal district commission of Canberra expended £850.000, and during the fiscal year 1926, which is the latest for which I have been able to get particulars, they spent £1,719,000, and as yet the government of Australia have not begun in any measure to erect the permanent structures for that capital. I submit that we in Canada should be and are equally proud of our capital, and we wish to see it second to none so far as the capitals of the dominions comprising the British Empire are concerned.
I would like to conclude with one further reason why I hope the house will not only accept the present proposal with regard to this capital expenditure of $3,000,000, but will accept it in a graceful and unanimous spirit. Last year we celebrated in Canada the sixtieth anniversary of confederation, and if that celebration evidenced anything it disclosed the pride taken by Canadians generally in their Dominion and in the capital of the Dominion. For the first time in the history of this country, every part of the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific was linked immediately with parliament hill; the voices of those who participated in that celebration in Ottawa were heard in all parts of our country. I do not think enough has been said of the work of the diamond jubilee celebration committee, in linking up at that time all parts of Canada with the capital. That phase of the celebration was largely undertaken by Hon. Thomas Aheam, who is the present chairman of the federal district commission. Mr. Aheam not only gave his services gratuitously to the work of that committee, but through his instrumentality that whole vast linking up of the Dominion from coast to coast was carried out, so I am informed, practically without the expenditure of a single dollar by
the committee. He was able to secure, as contributions towards that celebration from transportation companies, telephone companies, radio companies and electrical companies both in Canada and in the United States, all that was needed in the way of equipment and workmanship to make possible that exceptional feature of the celebration. The government feel that this country is fortunate in having Mr. Ahearn as the chairman of the federal district commission, and that we would be furthering the wishes of the people of Canada as a whole if, in connection with the diamond jubilee celebration, we could have through a further development in the beautification of this capital city some feature commemorative of that event, which might also serve as some recognition on the part of this generation of the work of the fathers of confederation. We of to-day have inherited these buildings and their surroundings, and we enjoy everything we have 'by way of their beauty and inspiration because of the work of those who preceded the present generation. II do not think we could more worthily honour the fathers of confederation and the vision which they had as to the future of Canada than by appropriating a sum sufficient to provide in the heart of this city, in connection with the celebration we had last year, a park which will be known to future generations as Confederation Park, and which will! be commemorative of that celebration and of the contribution made by this generation to the work of the fathers of confederation. I would ask hon. members of the house to believe that this was one of the objects which the government had in mind when they gave their sanction to the expropriations to which I have referred.
I should like to put on record one or two thoughts I have in regard to the _ future development of Ottawa as the capital of Canada. I believe no country in the world has been so fortunate as Canada in the natural beauty of its capital city, with its environs, its commanding position, its surrounding mountains and forests, its beautiful rivers. Ottawa is located by the side of a river, as is the case with many other capitals. London, as hon. members know, is situated on the banks of the Thames; Paris on the Seine; Rome on the Tiber; Washington on the Potomac, and other capital cities are similarly situated. None of these however, have in their rivers anything comparable to the Ottawa river into which flow, within the federal district the Rideau and Gatineau rivers. Running through the heart of this city there is also the Rideau canal, which to all intents and purposes is
2320	COMMONS
Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
a fine river in itself. I submit that the federal district commission should endeavour to secure both banks of all the river courses. Fortunately up to the present much of the banks of these rivers and the canal have been secured. Nothing could be done which would be more in the future interest of this city than to have the land along both sides of the Ottawa river acquired for public purposes, as far as it can be reasonably acquired, and in so far as that has not already been done. Similarly, there should be secured the land along both sides of the Rideau river and the Rideau canal. I am not saying this can be done, or that it will be done, but I think it should be done, and I think such a step would go far to make this capital what it should be in years to come. I also think, as I have already said, that the approach to parliament hill along Metcalfe street should be made more dignified, as befits this capital; that approach should be made two or three times its present width. I believe all the properties facing parliament Hill should be owned and controlled by this government in order to prevent structures being erected thereon which may destroy the harmony and beauty of the buildings on this hill. More than that-and this does not relate to the immediate present but to the future.-I believe there should be acquired in connection with this capital and the sooner the better a great tract of land, in the nature of a national park, which will be a fitting adjunct to the capital of our country. All this could be done to-day at a comparatively small cost and I believe that no investment the country could make would mean as much to the future of the capital of Canada as these particular developments if they are carried out.
There is one further step which I think will become necessary, namely that the capital of Canada be placed under the control of a federal district commission. When that step is to be taken is not for me to say at the moment. It might involve changes in the representation in parliament and might more appropriately be considered at a time when a redistribution measure is before the house. But I do think that sooner or later, and perhaps, having regard to the future, the sooner the better, this capital of the Dominion should be placed under the control of a federal district commission. The present action may prove a step in that direction.
Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that as we look upon the countries of the past and the countries bf the present, we find more and more reason to attach great significance to the

proper development of our capital. When we speak of ancient Greece we think of Athens and all that Athens stood for, and we judge of the character of the ancient Greeks largely by the types of buildings and what is left by way of remnants of architecture in that city which in the days of its greatness was the capital of Greece. When we think of the Roman Empire our thoughts turn to Rome and to what is there left of monuments of the past, as the embodiment of the spirit of that day. Similarly when we turn to other countries, to Great Britain, to the United States, to France, to Belgium, we see in what there is in architecture and in art in their capitals something symbolic of the genius of the peoples. So too with our Dominion; the capital is becoming increasingly the focal point of this great country. It is the point to which all eyes of this Dominion are turned; and not only that, but when people think of Canada it is to the capital of Canada that all eyes of the British Empire and of the world are turned. This capital is the seat of the government of the country. It should be and is something more than the seat of government. It is here at the capital of Canada that we have the residence of the representative of His Majesty the King. It is here that we have the official residence of the diplomatic representative of the nation to the south, the legation of the United States. It will be the future home of the diplomatic representatives of other countries as from time to time they come to have their respective representations and legations in Canada. It should be the home not only of government and of diplomacy in Canada, but it should also be and is in large measure already the home of the sciences and of art and of letters. We have in the city archives which are second to none of any country in the world. We have a national art gallery with art treasures of great value to this nation. We have a na- . tional museum which is an important national possession. We are planning at this time the development of important laboratories for scientific research. Our public buildings, as far as their architectural merits are concerned, are with few exceptions worthy of our country. In addition to the houses of parliament there are other public buildings which constitute exceptionally beautiful specimens of architecture, such as the Chateau Laurier, some of the churches, and I am happy also to say, some of the buildings erected by great companies. The Metropolitan Life Insurance Company's building, erected on lines of rare architectural beauty, is a building worthy of the great capital of this Dominion. We may

Federal District-Mr. Bennett
hope and I believe expect that other companies will follow the examples which have already been set.
We may not come to have the largest, the wealthiest, or the most cosmopolitan capital in the world, but I believe that with Ottawa's natural and picturesque setting, given stately proportions and a little careful planning, we can have the most beautiful capital in the worlld. So I would ask my fellow members of this House of Commons to view not only with sympathy but with enthusiasm a project which everyone will recognize as beyond any consideration of party, that has for its object solely and wholly the development and beautification of Ottawa as the capital of this great Dominion, something that will give some expression of all that is highest in the idealism of the nation, and something which those from beyond our gates and those who may follow in future years will come to recognize as an expression in some degree of the soul of the Canada of to-day.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to follow the right hon. the Prime Minister in his observations. I desire to congratulate him upon his conversion to the desirability of having parks in the city which is the capital city of our country; and his enthusiasm has all the zeal which characterizes the convert.
I recall that the park upon which the Chateau Laurier now stands was not invaded by a commercial enterprise without objection being taken by the Conservative party, and the speech which Sir George Foster made on that occasion will perhaps be recalled by the right hon. the Prime Minister.
We are now asked to spend over $1,500,000 to buy a park in the city of Ottawa to take the place of the park in which there has been built a hotel, and the use of which for commercial purposes was objected to by the opposition of that day. I mention that to the right hon. the Prime Minister in case he may have forgotten it.
The government of Sir Robert Borden, when it came into power in 1913, was fully seized of the desirability of beautifying Ottawa. I take it that there are very few people in Canada who are not desirous of making our capital worthy of the aspirations of the Canadian people. But when the government appointed a commission, known as the Holt commission, it was found that a very considerable sum of money would be necessary to carry out the proposed plans. That commission called to its assistance the very best expert advice which could be obtained, and
as a result plans were formulated, which doubtless have been inspected by nearly every member of this house.
The plan which has been laid before us to-day is a plan which is essentially not different from the plan which was thus prepared; in general outline it contemplates the same sort of development; but it was found that during the progress of the war it was impossible to spend the sums of money that would be involved.
May I say that this country is now suffer- [DOT] ing from a debt of two and a half billions of, dollars, while at that time it had a debt of less than four hundred millions. There is mot a gentleman on this side of the house, and I do not know of anyone in Canada, who is opposed to making this city a capital of great beauty, reflecting as I have already said in every sense the hopes and aspirations of the Canadian people. But there are other matters which must be considered. There is a very ancient saying that you must cut your garment according to your cloth. When the right hon. the Prime Minister referred to my observations last year, or the observations of the gentleman who led this party at that time he cannot have recently read them. I directed my attention to two points. One was that the operations of the commission should be extended, and the other was the desirability of having the commission representative in character; and I am happy to say that the right hon. the Prime Minister quite agreed with the observations made in that regard. Mr. Guthrie, it is perfectly true, urged the desirability of a larger expenditure being made than the annual sum which was contemplated by the bill, but that was all.
Now what are we asked to do? Suppose we get down to earth for a few moments and ask ourselves what we are proposing to do. We are proposing to vote $200,000 a year for thirty years, which is $6,000,000; and another $3,000,000 this year, which is $9,000,000 exclusive of interest and sinking fund. That may not be thought to be a large sum of money. We are so glibly talking of millions these days that I wonder where this country is going to end. I wonder if it is realized whait $3,000,000 means to the people of this country, what $3,000,000 would do in bringing happiness and delight and some measure of creature comforts to men and women on the prairies, what it would do to men and women who find it very difficult to struggle under the conditions under which they now live, what it would do with respect to health and all the matters that are allied to the health of a nation. There is something more than the

Federal District-Mr. Bennett
beauty of the capital and that is the health of its people. When we have seen, as I have, conditions that exist in some parts of this country because of the long distances men and women are from transportation and other facilities, we should reflect carefully as to what the reasons were that made it impossible for us to spend this money in 1913. We had a debt then of less than $400,000,000; we had bouyant revenues, and it is not an easy thing now, when we have a debt of $2,500,000,-JOOO that is not being reduced in my judgment as it should, to ask the country to vote these large sums of money.
I am wholly in accord with the desirability of beautifying Ottawa. Is there any man who is not? It is the capital of Canada and the distinction between the city of Ottawa and the capital of Canada was one well taken by the Prime Minister but we cannot always have the things we should like to have. How many of us can always have what we want? There are in this country men and women who have artistic minds, as mentioned by the Prime Minister, but they cannot gratify their tastes and aspirations. The problem is a simple one. Can the Canadian people at this moment afford to enter upon the venture proposed by the Prime Minister? He has already made commitments of over $1,500,000 for the Russell hotel and other buildings behind it, that will involve total expenditures, according to the resolution, of $3,000,000. The Prime Minister was very frank the other day when he said that there would be required $150,000 per annum for maintenance and $50,000 per annum for general improvements that are made from year to year. So we must pay the interest upon $3,000,000 for a venture which is not intended to be revenue-producing. Therefore it will cost us something like $350,000 a year and at the end of the period we must pay the $3,000,000. I yield to no man in my desire to see this the city beautiful; but if in my older years I have become a bit practical, I think the Prime Minister will excuse me when I say that I am not disposed to enter upon large projects without at least having some idea of what is involved in money expenditures and what it means to the people who have to pay.
It is all very nice to talk about posterity raising monuments to your memory and about the right hon. member's biography being a delightful volume showing his vision and his desire to see this city what it should be; but after all, who has to pay the money? In 1958 the Minister of Finance of that day will have to provide $3,000,000 or somebody must in the meantime provide the money to pay

it. There is just this further word to be said about the details of the measure. It is most unsound as a piece of national financing. It authorizes a commission to issue securities which the country must pay. Why should we hand over to somebody else the power to make expenditures with our money? The resolution states that out of the consolidated revenues these moneys may be paid and further that the Minister of Finance will provide the money to pay the interest and sinking funds. Is he going to include this as part of the national debt? Is this to be part of the obligations of the country? As I say, this is not a revenue-producing venture and if it were not objectionable-I believe it is a proper term-I would say that this is a form of deception practised upon the Canadian people by which a commission issues its securities guaranteed by the people of this country, on which securities the people have to pay out of their own revenues the interest and sinking fund. In other words, the people of Canada are putting their money into this venture to the extent of $3,000,000 capital and $200,000 a year for thirty years for maintenance and improvements, or a total of $9,000,000. That is the story short and simple, and my only difficulty is: Can we afford it?
The Prime Minister no doubt will say: It is a very small sum of money; the gentlemen who prepared this plan, the Holt commission, in their scheme for a central park contemplated in part these expenditures. It is a very desirable thing, but no nation can have all the things it now desires. Great as Great Britain is and rich as the city of London is, they did not at one step expropriate the land fronting on the Strand in order to widen that thoroughfare. Those who have seen the operations that went on there realize that they were carried on from year to year. As buildings grew old and had to be replaced by new buildings, they provided that the street line should be so many feet behind the present line in order that there might be a widening of the thoroughfare. The Kingsway is a new highway that was built from Constitution hill down to the heart of the city, but the city of London has done the work gradually. There is a big jog by the Tivoli; then there is a straight line and another jog, and wherever a new building is put up there is a widening of the thoroughfare.
Cannot we afford to proceed in this way in Canada, having regard to what our position is? I think so. I do not for one moment underestimate the financial position of this country; but when the Prime Minister referred to the men being short-sighted who

Federal District-Mr. Bennett
laid out these buildings, I can only say that possibly they were short-sighted but it must be remembered that at that time they were dealing with a very exceptional and difficult position. If as a result of that we are now to denounce them as short-sighted, what would you say with respect to those who in 1908 took a portion of the park and gave it for an hotel? That only took place in the year 1908 and I have under my hand the debate that occurred on that occasion on the 6th day of July. That was only twenty years ago and of course twenty years make a great difference in one's attitude, especially if one has had greater responsibilities. It is pleasing to know that the government of the day, now led by the Prime Minister, is desirous so far as possible of maintaining parks whereas in those days the desire was to put hotels on them. That is what happened in twenty years and, if that be so, it may well be that those who come after us twenty years hence will say that the Prime Minister was extravagant in his proposal. If these men in 1867 were short-sighted under the circumstances I have mentioned and if in twenty years the Prime Minister has had a change of heart and desires to provide a park for that taken from the people of Canada, to put an hotel upon, against the protest of leading public men of that day-if there has been this change in twenty years and we now are seeking to buy a park at a cost of millions of dollars- it is possible that another change may take place whereby people will say that in this regard we are'grossly extravagant.
I will not offer any further observations except to the Minister of Finance. If he will read the bill I am sure that he will say that it is unsound financing. Why do we not make appropriations as they do in Ontario in regard to parks? The parks commission lays down a five-year plan; it submits its estimates to the. government every year; the government approves them and the appropriations are voted by the legislature. This idea of getting away from the responsibility of parliament is against the whole principle of responsible government about which the Prime Minister used to talk so much. I notice a great change between the Prime Minister in power and in opposition. Orders in council are now the order of the day. In the days of opposition they used to be denounced most roundly and vigorously. Now instead of accepting the responsibility of parliament with respect to expenditures, leaving the house to decide how much money we shall annually put into parks, we are making commitments
for the present and for the future that divest this parliament of responsibility with respect to these expenditures. I say essentially that is unsound. It is not in accordance with the theory of responsible government. It is not in accordance with the theory on which Ontario operates its magnificent park at Niagara Falls. That commission lays out its plans; it makes up its budgets; it determines what money shall be paid over a period of years and the way in which the improvements are to be made; it goes to the legislature asking for appropriations; the government puts the appropriations before the legislature in order that, having regard to the financial condition of the province, they may determine what action they will take, and never yet has that commission been unable to carry out its plans as they should be carried out. I do submit that all this legislation divesting parliament of its responsibility, all this placing of money in the hands of commissions, all this authorizing of commissions to raise money on the credit of the Canadian people, for the Minister of Finance knows it is upon the credit of the Canadian people either directly, or indirectly, with guarantees in some cases and moral obligations in others-all this is a negation of the whole principle of responsible government under which we live. I ask the Minister of Finance-I know his government is sufficiently powerful to put this measure through-to recast these financial provisions to provide that this expenditure shall be a direct payment of the Canadian people to this commission, for we never hope to get the money back. The commission had no money with which to pay the interest except the money we give them; that is clear. We do not expect to get the money back; it is not intended that we should; it is not intended that they should pay interest on the money except in so far as we provide them with the money with which to do it. The bill itself makes that point so clear that there can be no difficulty over it. But I do ask the Minister of Finance to put this matter on a sound financial basis if the thing is to be done at all.
I for one do not object to any reasonable expenditures being made to beautify this capital. I am anxious that we should beautify it, but I am also anxious that the beautification should be made in accordance with our present capacity to pay for it, having regard to the demands that are insistently being made upon us by every branch of the public service. We are doing fairly well by Ottawa, I think, and we have been doing so.
Federal District-Mr. Bennett

We cannot do it all in a single day. We cannot tear down public buildings and turn the area into a beautiful public park just because we feel it is a beautiful thing to do.
The Prime Minister referred to the beauties of Greece and the glories of Rome, but I venture to say to him and to this house that Greece and Rome are not remembered by the buildings they put up. The beauties of Greece and the glories of Rome are remembered by the men they produced, by the laws they made, by the philospohy and the literature they created-not by their buildings. That is not the thing by which these ancient civilizations have been remembered. It is true that the Pyramids and the Sphinx are an enduring monument to Egyptian civilization, that the hanging gardens of Babylon are a monument to Babylonian beauty, that the ruins of the Parthenon and the Colosseum recall the grandeur of Athenian and Roman civilizations, but it is not upon the architectural glories of Greece and Rome, but upon their contributions to the liberty and freedom of mankind, that their great place in history rests. Their laws, their literature, their philosophy, these are the things by which they are remembered, and I say to the Prime Minister that if he thinks by going out and spending money tearing down buildings and laying out a public park, and improving the approaches to this building, we are going to make a permanent contribution to the civilization of Canada, he is very much mistaken. Canada will be judged in the eyes of mankind by the type of men and women we produce, by the laws we enact, by the care we have exercised for those who are dependent upon this country. These are the factors by which our civilization will be judged, and not by material evidence. That at least is my submission.
I have tried to make it abundantly clear on every occasion on which I have spoken of the matter that I yield to no man in my desire to see a beautiful capital in Canada, but I have to regulate my desire for beauty by my financial ability to pay for it, and I ask the ministry to pause before they commit us to this plan of financing, and to all these expenditures, without due regard to our present capacity to pay. I wonder if it is realized by hon. gentlemen opposite-sometimes I think it is not-that in these days when the burden of taxation is so great-why, only this morning I saw a letter from a gentleman who said that he was not going to remain on the Canadian side of the border, but cross over to the other

side, "for on my gross income of 816,000," he said, "I pay over 1700 in taxes in Canada, and on the other side I would have to pay 76 per cent less."
A real patriot.
