Yes. I think that we
should make only such appropriations for the beautification of Ottawa as our present and immediate future financial position permits, having regard to the claims that are urgently made upon us by every branch of the public service. Until we have passed the stage where railway deficits are annually recurrent, until we have reached the point where our railways are earning sufficient money to pay the interest on their obligations, is it quite fair that we should ask this added obligation to be borne by the Canadian people? I am speaking for myself, because this is not a controversial matter in any sense of the term, and my own personal view would be, if I had the responsibility, to expend such sums as my financial position would permit, and to increase them as my financial resources warranted, But having regard to our present financial condition, and in view of the demands that are so insistently made upon us from every part of, this country for public accommodation, for post offices, custom houses, and public buildings of 'every kind, in communities that have been without proper accommodation for years, and whioh are now crying out for public buildings, as well as the need for accommodation in the new communities that are being opened up, can we proceed with this venture and forego these very necessary things merely in order to have the capital beautified?
The Prime Minister used one word-he used it twice-and if he will apply it, then my

Federal District-Mr. Evans
support of this undertaking will be very much more readily given. He used the word sacrifice. He said they were willing to make the sacrifice. When it is explained to me just what sacrifice the government of this country is making in public expenditures to create this park and make these improvements, my mind will be very much more at rest. Has anybody seen any evidence of sacrifice? Where are they? What are the sacrifices? It was that one word that fastened itself upon my attention as the Prime Minister proceeded. He spoke of other cities, of other capitals, of other nations, of other people, and of the money they had spent, and he spoke of what has been done in this country, and of the willingness of the people to make a sacrifice for beauty, a sacrifice for the capital. When I am given some evidence of the sacrifice contemplated by this government, it will be much more easy for me to accommodate myself to the expenditure.

I shall
not take more than a few minutes, but I wish to say a word on this question. I congratulate the Prime Minister on his presentation of his case, but frankly I am opposed to the whole thing, for reasons which I shall try to make clear. In criticizing the scheme, I would say in the first place that we have no business under any conditions to go across Wellington street. I think it would have been much better had we acquired some of the buildings there, cleared them away and beautified the street, instead of going across to Sparks street. Then some of us might be able to approach this house without taking our lives in our hands. But my main opposition to the scheme is for the reason that it is out of harmony with the crude way in which our people have to make their living and furnish the income of this nation. Take our roads, for example. Thousands of our people to-day, west of the great lakes, are not able to get to the post office for their mail for weeks in the springtime. Then perhaps no country in the world is so crude as to its methods of travel, and every day, particularly every weekend, we have a list of casualties at level crossings. Some of our money might well be spent at this time in removing that menace to highway travel. Then again we need expenditure on branch lines, so necessary throughout certain parts of the country. I am sure that those of our people who are without railway facilities will not become enthusiastic over a scheme of this kind, however much they would like to be. Then I recall many of our soldiers throughout
the Dominion suffering from their war service, but who have never yet been able to get on the pension list. I could name 6ome of them off-hand if required. They should be looked after by the country, having faced death in the battle line for our protection. I know of one man to-day who has been in hospital for two years as a result of his war experience, but he has not yet been able to secure a pension. I am sure hon. members generally will recall that only last year the Minister of Finance himself, when asked if some of our civil servants whose wages were below the living line could not be granted an increase of pay, said, "It is time somebody spoke on 'behalf of the taxpayer." Are we then to spend every year the large sum provided for in this bill, and entrust the money to a body of men who are not even responsible to parliament? And what about the national debt? Surely before making unecessary expenditures in the manner proposed, we should do something to reduce that debt and so make it easier for the national revenue to be raised each year.
Now, I should like to have fallen in with this scheme enthusiastically, for I take second place to no one in my desire for the beautification of our capital, but, as I have already said, this scheme is out of keeping with the crude way in which some of our people have to live. Let me point out that in some of our towns in western Canada to-day-I have in mind particularly a good-sized town of three thousand inhabitants in my own constituency-there is mot a government building in which a cabinet minister would house his motor oar-not one. The whole cabinet is taking a most inconsistent position in asking the country enthusiastically to adopt this scheme.
I come from west of the great lakes, from a part of the country that is not even allowed to own its public resources; and yet we are asked to approve of a scheme like this. I say it is utterly inconsistent. We are not even allowed the property that belongs to us as a province, and yet we are expected to tax ourselves to provide means for the beautification of this city by making a central park and other improvements. I repeat, the Prime Minister and his cabinet under these conditions is occupying a most inconsistent position.
The Prime Minister has spoken of the public buildings of some of the other provinces, but they cannot all be cited as parallel cases. The public buildings in Regina are surrounded by land on which our settlers cannot make a living. And yet every day we

Federal District-Mr. Church
are spending money to encourage immigration, when the conditions created by the concentration of wealth and industry in our cities have driven our people off the land. This scheme to beautify the capital of Canada is in accordance with the policy that has been followed in this country for many yeans past of concentrating everything in the cities at the expense of the rural districts. Until those conditions are changed, I say to the Prime Minister across the floor of this house that he cannot expect the agriculturists of western Canada to accept this scheme enthusiastically.
I have nothing further to say, Mr. Speaker, but I would have been remiss in my duty had I not pointed out some of the conditions under which the government expect to secure the money for this scheme.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the country will support the fair and just stand taken by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The principle of the bill is all wrong. When this commission was created in 1899 the Prime Minister said it was for the purpose of making Ottawa the Washington of the north. Well, it has become the Washington of the north. It was intended then to work up to making Ottawa a federal district. In fact this whole country has become the Mexico of the north with our new status and as a happy hunting ground for the millionaires of the United States in possessing themselves of ' our resources. There is no city on the North American continent to-day of anything like the same size and population that has as extensive a park area or as large expenditures on its beautification by the federal government, by the city council and by other public agencies as the city of Ottawa.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the principle of the bill is all wrong. We all want to see this a beutiful city, we all are favourable to liberal expenditure by the federal authorities ou some definite plan for its beautification, but those expenditures must not be in excess of what the country can afford and a lot of it should wait. The Ottawa improvement commission has been functioning for thirty years or since 1899. With what result? The same old streets covered with snow and ice, the same old water supply, the same old way of doing things that in any business enterprise would spell bankruptcy. Every year the Dominion contributes to the municipality the equivalent of five or six mills of the local taxation, and the financial burden and liability of the taxpayers of Ottawa is distributed over the taxpayers of the whole Dominion. Do not forget that a very large amount of

money is spent here every year. Nearly every large public federal building has a park around it. Take the expenditures on the Victoria musuem, and also the expenditures on the experimental farm, Rideau canal, and, further, the expenditures by the Canadian National Railways, by the Canadian Pacific Railway, by the city itself, by the school board and by this commission, running into many millions of dollars. The other day a return brought down showed that several hundred thousand dollars have been spent by the government over a period of years in renting office space in private buildings throughout the city-buildings that nobody else would rent owing to the economic situation here. It would be a far better plan if the government would improve the salaries of the underpaid people in the Post Office and the other government departments and the civil service in general and so help them to pay their rent and taxes and to get a fair day's pay for a fair day's work in Ottawa.
I am not opposing personally the gentlemen composing the commission. They are all public-spirited gentlemen, but their way of doing business is in my opinion deplorable. As an illustration of this, in 1912 they sent out an illustrated booklet showing a large number of small parks and driveways throughout the city! and the expenditures that had been made on these improvements. I can show you cement walks, roadways, gradings and driveways built by this commission all over Ottawa where there is considerable poor workmanship and the life of the work has been only ten years; and yet they have issued bonds for thirty-five years. The result is that at the end of the thirty-five years you will find that what should cost SI.20 a cubic yard will cost S3 and SI a yard as the case may be.
As a result of criticism the government has marked down the proposed increase in maintenance charges from $2'5O,OO0 to $200,000. Here we have a total expenditure of some $9,000,000- $6,000,000, or $200,000 a year for thirty years, plus $3,000,000 capital expenditure-for the beautifying of Ottawa. And what has been done? They have destroyed the continuity of the Sparks street district, where the bulk of the business assessment in the city exists. Sparks street as a commercial thoroughfare has been destroyed. They have torn down warehouses and commercia' buildings and ruined the street in order to create a park, in what should be an industrial district. There you have warehouses and railways sidings, with a canal at the doors of two railway systems, and I contend that these frontages should not be used for

Federal District-Mr. Church
the purpose now intended but left for a great industrial district. This is not Washington. Washington is the capital of a country with a population of 110,000,000, whereas in this country we have a population of 10,000,000. I believe other municipalities of the country do not approve of this expenditure or of this policy of spending money like water. Originally in 1899 it was proposed to make Ottawa a federal district; if that were done the capital would then have the power to levy taxation for such purposes as this and we would have cleaner streets, a better water supply and lower city taxes. The city of Washington is a federal district which has powers of taxation, but this commission has no such powers; it receives no revenues. The result is that bonds have to be issued for every little bit of work that is done over maintenance. If walks have to be built and a little more gardening done, bonds have to be issued for a period of thirty years or thirty-five years-and this at the high cost of money which has prevailed in the past few years.
I cannot find anything comparable to this federal assistance measure in any city in the world. A subvention here is given to the municipality in exchange for property exemption from taxation and for the use of the police and the fire departments. Many other provincial capitals have asked for subventions from the provinces but have not been able to get them. From Victoria to Halifax the various capitals in this Dominion are contributing to the governments of the provinces. Winnipeg, for instance, maintains a police force and fire department but does not receive a dollar in the way of subvention in exchange for these services directly. Nor is there anything like this in Great Britain. In New South Wales the city of Sydney, the capital of the state, gets a million and a half a year, equal to the cost of maintaining the police force or the fire department. Melbourne has a subvention from the state gov-erment, as has also Wellington, New Zealand, in exchange for civic services. There are no state subventions in the United States in connection with the beautification of the state capital, and I find none in the British Empire. It seems to me that sooner or later, in the interests of efficiency and economy, Ottawa must be taken over and made a federal district.
There is a great deal of criticism of the purchase of the old Russell house site at a cost of more than a million dollars, a fabulous sum, in respect of which no tenders were called for. And only a small part of the property has been taken over. Those
who negotiated the transaction got their heads together and agreed to a price of $1,125,000 for property which should certainly have been the subject of an arbitration. The matter should have been referred to a board of arbitration and the value of the land and buildings proved.
Talk about beautifying the capital! Why, as a result of the recent fire there is a wall in front of the Russell building which may fall down on a street car on Sparks street at any time, and no attempt is being made either by the government or by the city of Ottawa to remove the danger. The city architect has the power by law to send someone in at once to remove that menace, and to charge the cost to the owner of the building, but nothing has been done to safeguard the public. Ottawa is called by some of the newspapers-the Stratford Beacon and Globe among them-the mendicant city, and editorials have contended that the country cannot afford the expenditure of money along the lines here proposed or to build a new museum' or court building to house the supreme court, as the Evening Journal suggests.
This federal district commission seems to be giving away things. About a month or two ago the chairman of this commission, who is also the head of the Ottawa Electric Company, a private concern which gets about two-thirds of the electrical business of the city, at higher rates than those charged by the hydro-electric, the peoples' own system, proposed to give away eleven acres of quasi civic property at Rockliffe. To whom? To Mr. Phillips, the United States ambassador, for a residence. That is not the way we should deal with public property. No member of the commission would give away his own property that way.

Federal District-Mr. Church

If the Prime Minister will read the minutes of the board of control and city council of the city of Ottawa he will see that this commission has power to take over that civic leasehold property, which it occupied at a rental under a written civic lease. It was proposed to give that property away and a meeting was held at the city hall of people protesting against any such action. I am not aware of the government of the United States giving away public property in Washington.
In connection with this commission, as I have pointed out, we are faced with an expenditure of 19,000,000, while we have to meet an expenditure of $2,500,000 in London on account of Canada House, with maintenance amounting to $130,000 and half a million for a Washington embassy-all this while the people are groaning under heavy taxation. The government is spending money like water; that is all that can be said of this commission.
I submit that the purchase of this particular Russell house property should be looked ' into by the public accounts committee, and all expenditures of the commission should be similarly investigated. As a matter of fact, in my opinion, the commission should be abolished and its work taken over by the government of Canada. The government does not seem able to clean its own streets on parliament hill any better than Ottawa cleans its streets. The condition of the streets in the immediate vicinity of this building is a disgrace to the city of Ottawa. The Department of Public Works have been so incompetent and have so neglected this condition that one of the most popular members on this side of the house has fallen and seriously injured himself. If the government would only try to provide the citizens. of Ottawa with a proper water supply, and make some effort to have the streets cleaned, it would be far better than spending money on this commission in the way it is doing.
Those are not all the expenditures which are proposed; it has been suggested that we should have a new art gallery and new supreme court building, with extensive grounds surrounding it, and that idea is supported by this wonderful paper, the Evening Journal, which has done so much for my friends on the other side of the house. Every time the Journal supports our party in Ottawa we go under, when the ballot boxes are opened. This paper seems to be the mouthpiece of this federal district commission; in the old

days it supported the suggestion that Ottawa should be the Washington of the north, but when it was proposed that the hydro-electric commission should extend its activities to the Ottawa valley to break up the monopoly which then existed, this paper opposed the suggestion on election day where it is best known. I think it would be far better to beautify this city by bringing in industries which will help to keep our young men here and provide opportunities for jobs in Ottawa by a proper economic policy. I have heard a good deal of complaint from a few of the retail business men of Ottawa because the government propose to spoil the continuity of Sparks street, which should be one of the greatest retail districts in Canada. This commission has been criticized many times because of the way it buys real estate, going out to buy with a brass band; it first announces that it is going to buy some property, and all the real estate agents get busy and get there first. That is not the way to buy real estate to-day; that is not the way private owners or business men buy it and that is not the way the hydroelectric commission buy it.
We are told that we are to have a wonderful park known as Confederation park, but I believe the people of Canada have had enough expenditures of that kind within the last year or so on confederation fads. This government sent 750,000 men out of Canada; they did not celebrate Confederation day in this country on July 1st last, but took part in the fourth of July proceedings in the United States. Charity should begin at home, and Ottawa would be far better off if it had a few industries, together with a proper economic policy with cheap light and power. That would be better than squandering millions of dollars on such a scheme as this, which could well wait for a few years. I venture to say that if a committee of the house were to go over the estimates and public accounts they would find thousands of dollars which should be spent by the taxpayers of Ottawa but which has to be borne by the taxpayers of Canada. The principle of the bill is all wrong; if it is desired to make Ottawa a federal district, well and good. That was what Sir Wilfrid Laurier proposed in 1899; he wanted to take the city over on that basis, collect the taxes and beautify the city, but that idea was never carried into effect. To-day we have a federal district commission, but this is not a district at all; it is still a municipality. Look at the Rideau canal at the end of Sparks street; on one side we have a shipbuilding yard, and when you look over the wall you see a lot of stone hookers, old dilapidated dredges and

Federal District-Mr. Chevrier
scows lying there under repair. I was asked the other day if that was the first unit of Canada's navy, which was supposed to be locked up in some garage in Halifax. I am sure that is a thing of beauty and a joy forever; so on with the good work of beautifying the capital! No doubt this work is very near and very dear to the heart of the Prime Minister, but I cannot agree with the principle of the measure.

Mr. Speaker, with the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister I am heartily in accord, and consequently I will not have very much to say. It is a very great privilege indeed for me, together with my distinguished colleague, to represent in this house the city of Ottawa. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, this is the capital city of the Dominion, so I would rather speak as one of the members representing in this parliament the capital city of Canada. I think I can safely do so because under British parliamentary procedure once a member of parliament has taken his seat he is not so much concerned with parochial or local matters, but is bound to look at questions as they affect the general welfare of the entire country. So, under these conditions, I would speak as one whose privilege it is to represent the capital city of Canada rather than the city of Ottawa.
Ottawa, as is the case with other cities, is administered by a municipal government and is under the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario. I may say that the city council of Ottawa and the provincial government of Ontario have done well by this city. At the same time, this is the capital city of Canada, and just as there are obligations devolving upon the municipal council and the provincial government with respect to this city, so I submit there are obligations devolving upon this national body with regard to this capital city. No one would appreciate it more and no one would be happier than I should this amount of money which I believe we can afford to spend-since the Minister of Finance has seen fit to let the resolution go on the order paper-be distributed for the individual good of those in this country who deserve and need it. Nobody more than myself would like to see that amount of money paid out to those who have returned from overseas and who are now in a painful condition. But the Department of Health is looking after the national health; the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is looking after the painful cases, and what other systems, I ask, could be devised whereby this amount of money could be distributed to the
individuals who might benefit therefrom? If such a scheme is feasible; if any hon. gentleman who is opposed to this measure simply because he thinks this amount of money could be spent in a more worthy cause were to devise means to accomplish that end, then, Mr. Speaker, I would vote against this resolution; otherwise I say there that a national obligation devolves upon parliament to look after the capital city of Ottawa as befits this country. This parliament building is but a few years old; many years were spent in its construction. Those who conceived the plans and directed the building of it thought they were looking far into the future, but it has not taken long, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the foresight of those charged with the construction of this building, to demonstrate that it is even now too small to meet the demands of this growing nation. And what will happen in a few years? So when we come to talk about foresight, we must look further ahead than say twenty-five or fifty years, even fifty or one hundred years, when it comes to matters of national importance.
We have been told, Mr. Speaker, that Rome and Greece are remembered not by the buildings they erected, not by the splendour of their architecture. But just as the literature of a country reflects the sentiments, the hopes, the ambitions and the desires of its people, so the character of the public buildings, the meeting places of the councils of the nation, the places where the destiny of a country is determined, will indicate to the people of the future whether or not these were people of culture. And it ill behooves anyone, sir, to say at this time of our national life that men and women whose names could be put down to-day will not be regarded by future generations as men and women of culture. And if we remember these countries because of their culture, we remember them also for the tangible evidences handed down to us of their contributions to art, whether in the form of sculpture, or of painting, or by their crude manner of erecting pyramids or other monuments of national importance in their day. So that on that score the argument against this resolution cannot stand.
. We will suppose that there are other ways in which we could spend this money, probably in the construction of post offices and in the improvement of other public buildings. Somebody spoke of consistency. Let it be made evident, then, when any proposals for the spending of money on these public buildings or the improvement of other public works come up for consideration, that those who to-day say that there ought to be consistency

I am not disputing
that, but the hon. gentleman should put that up to the government of the province from which he comes. Roads, unless they are international highways, are altogether within the jurisdiction of the provincial government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is very little more for me to say. What I ask is that this subject be viewed with the same broadness with which it has been conceived. There are obligations towards the capital city. We are told we should do as has been done in London, that we should proceed slowly. Since the institution of the Ottawa improvement commission in 1898-it is now the federal district commission-moneys have been voted to it by parliament for the beautification of the capital city.
We are told that in England matters of this kind progress rather slowly; that old buildings are bought and made the basis of future gradual development. There are no old buildings that can- be bought here. The Russell house, which has been destroyed by fire, is the only old building that now stands in the way of this development, and if we are to wait until all the buildings involved are moss covered and so dilapidated that they are apt to tumble down on our heads, there will be no beautification at all.
For the reasons which the right hon. the Prime Minister advanced, as well as for those I have ventured to offer at this time, I intend to support the motion.

ME -Speaker, there are only one or two observations I would make. I placed myself on record in opposition to this proposal last year, and I desire to do so again. It is all very well to speak o-f our national obligations to Ottawa as the capital of the

Dominion of Canada. It is true that those obligations exist, and we all must give some consideration to them, but there are other obligations besides those that are related to the city of Ottawa. As long as this goes on I do not see much chance of getting that post office that I want in Sydenham. Why should hon. gentlemen smile over a matter as serious as that? Some of those who smile are expecting buildings or public works in their own constituencies. Does the government owe nothing to the parts of the country outside of Ottawa where works were undertaken or promised fourteen or fifteen years ago but held up by the war? Must nearly every dollar you have to spend be sunk in embassies at Washington, Tokyo or Paris, and the remainder, if any, spent in tearing down city blocks in the city of Ottawa? The Prime Minister has indicated that what he has in mind is to tear down all the city between (Metcalfe and O'Connor street from Wellington right down -I do not know how far down. I suppose you would not stop short of Queen street, would you? It is indicated that that is the picture he has in his mind. How beautiful it would be to get rid of those buildings and have an avenue of trees approaching this building! For that matter, how much is to be added to the attractiveness of these buildings by tearing down the city blocks opposite? Get outside of this building, and how much can you see? You would have to have a neck as long as a giraffe to see it. When a park takes the place of the city block, nothing will be added to the beauty of this place. Some years ago, under the federal plan back in 1913, a certain amount of money was spent. As has been said, that was at a time when our national debt was comparatively small, very small as compared with the debt of to-day. Frog ponds were filled up, beautiful drives were made-and some people in Ottawa added considerably to their fortunes when- those projects were being put through. Some became comparatively wealthy men through the changes that were produced in Ottawa by the construction of those drives and the beautifying of that part of the city. I venture to say that there are some who are very directly interested in the tearing down of whole city blocks and who will not be any poorer because of the part they have played in that regard. I protest again against an expenditure of this kind, against the government of the day underbaking to place in the hands of a commission, composed of men who are not responsible to parliament, the expenditure of money over a period of thirty years. It would be bad enough if it were done

Federal District-Mr. Dunning
for a period of four or five years, but to commit those on whose shoulders will rest the responsibility of administering this country thirty years hence by tying up moneys in this way is in my judgment a very wrong principle and one to which I cannot give my support. My hon. friend from Ottawa says in regard to roads: Oh, that is a provincial matter. It is not a provincial matter as regards miles and miles of roads just outside of Ottawa across the river through the city of Hull. That is being taken care of by this government. Roads which run for miles out of the city and which ought to be under provincial control are being constructed and maintained with money advanced by the Dominion of Canada. They are not provincial roads. Where it suits the purpose of those who have the beautification of Ottawa in mind, they can make Dominion roads out of roads which are miles outside the city, and even across the river, under the plea that they are doing this all in order to add to the beauty of the city of Ottawa. The whole principle in my judgment is wrong and I desire to protest as I did last year.

It means that at the present time the people oif Canada are expending through the federal commission, for tihe purpose of beautifying this city, approximately two and one-haif cents per head per annum, and the proposal now before us, if carried out in its entirety and allowing for the capitalization oif the interest upon the $3,000,000 of the capital sum, will involve how much per head? As a matter of practical fact what does history teach us with regard to these matters? The history of every national capital wherever located teaches us this, that there are always those who, in the interest of economy and sincerely believing as the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) does, that the expenditure is not necessary and not wise, oppose such expenditures. But history also teaches us in connection with every national capital that succeeding generations

pay many millions more than would have been paid had sufficient foresight been displayed earlier in the history of the capital.
I am pleased to say that Regina, the capital of the province which I have the honour to represent, has not been subject to that handicap because we were fortunate in having as the first premier of Saskatchewan a man of really broad vision with respect to the future of his province and its capital city. The Hon. Walter Scott was for a number of years a member of this house and subsequently he became the first premier of Saskatchewan. He put through, in the face of considerable opposition, the purchase of a large tract of what was then farm land outside of the city of Regina and he proceeded there to erect a provincial capital which is to-day the pride of all the people of Saskatchewan. As a consequence of that vision on the part of the Hon. Walter Scott, expenditures for the purposes of the provincial capital of Saskatchewan are lower than they are in the case of any of the other western provinces. That is due to the fact that vision was displayed at the start and a comprehensive plan arrived at. Let me take by contrast the province of Manitoba, which has a beautiful parliament building, located on a site altogether too small and with no approach. Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg are to-day spending large sums of money to clear the approaches to their parliament buildings. In the city of Toronto constant expenditures are necessary in order to remedy conditions such as exist there. I deprecate very strongly the exaggeration of the cost of this proposal to the individual taxpayer of Canada. The cost is easily ascertainable and, as I have indicated, it is less than four cents per head per annum of the population of Canada for the next thirty years. May I point out that those of us who have to cross these streets that are being dealt with, Wellington street and Sparks street, are becoming more and more interested personally in some improvement in traffic conditions, and the provision of more room for traffic, in order that we may have a chance to cross those streets and continue to live. The plan which is now before parliament, drafted by the federal district commission, is such as to indicate that better traffic conditions and greater public safety were taken into account in its preparation.
My hon. friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans) referred to the necessity for expenditure on level crossings. I have on the order paper a resolution which I hope to have dealt with to-day, and upon which a bill will be based, which has in view a greater use of the grade

crossing fund. All these matters are related and must be considered together. I look at the question of the improvement and beautification of Ottawa from a business point of view, and having in mind the experience of other capitals in that regard, I say that if we do not undertake this work to-day, substantially on the basis outlined, the people of Canada will in the future have to pay a great deal more for doing the very thing which is now under discussion, and will in all likelihood spend throughout the year, in connection with enterprises of a similar character, much greater sums than are mentioned here. As my hon. friend from Rosetown was speaking I was reminded of the city in which he lives, Saskatoon. If the people of Saskatoon had been moved in their early history and in their subsequent development by the arguments which the hon. member for Rosetown has advanced to-day, there would not be there that beautiful city, there would not be there that great university, there would not be on every hand the expression of a people's pride in the country which they had helped to build up.	That is, after all, what we are doing
here. We are just doing our little bit; it is not a very big bit. Are we justified in committing the people of Canada to spend four cents per head each year for the next thirty years in making this capital a little more like wh'at it ought to be as representative of the Canadian people?

I am in favour of this bill because of my conviction that the beautification of our public property is a form of national self-expression which we cannot afford to neglect. It is all very well to talk about the mental and moral achievements of the classic nations of days gone by, but however great they may have been, we must understand that what they achieved was not done in a vacuum. It was produced through the interaction between those peoples and their environment, progressively producing around themselves objects of enduring beauty. I feel that no people, especially a people like we are, can very long be denied its instinct for just this form of self-realization. After all, I think that public buildings and public parks, when accomplished along lines of true artistic merit, become the only kind of depository possible to us whereby we can pass on to future generations any mental and moral achievements we may attain. I cannot see how we can build up any bridge between ourselves and the future unless somehow we crystallize our mental gains into objective beauty of some form.

Federal District-Mr. Bird
I happened to read a short while ago a book which very materially corrected my impressions about the wonderful architecture which is scattered throughout the British Isles, and which to-day forms such a strong attraction for the moneyed people of this continent. I was under the impression that these old churches and public buildings which you encounter in England about every three miles along the rural highways were produced out of the superflous wealth of the rich merchants of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries-produced, in other words, by sweated labour. I always imagined that the mortar that binds those blocks of stone together was somehow mingled with the blood of people in a state of semi-slavery, but I learned from this book that these beautiful churches were actually built by the people themselves. The wonderful stone work was done by the village mason; the beautiful wood carving was done by the village carpenter, and even the church bells were foundered at the village smithy. The whole structure from foundation to spire tip was produced locally, and these local artisans were paid by an impost made locally upon the people of the community. It is a beautiful self-expression of the character of a great people in the first stages of its formation, and all the wealth of character that we associate with the English people has been passed on to us by this means, and by no other. We must understand that the achievements of a nation with regard to character and mental acquisitions are cumulative. We cannot produce in one generation all that we aspire to be, but from generation to generation we must seek some artistic form of self-expression whereby we can effectively pass on to future generations that which we have achieved morally and intellectually.
Another thing. After all, these public improvements which we seek to make worthy of ourselves are a matter for the public. That is to say, we can achieve collectively that which we cannot achieve individually. Personally I am very fond of reading that famous essay of Bacon on Gardens, and I never read it without thinking that if I were a man of means that is precisely the kind of garden I would have around my home; but of course one would have to be a millionaire to achieve such an ideal. Here by the simple process of national co-operation we can produce in Ottawa, in Winnipeg, in Saskatoon, or in Calgary this very ideal of which Bacon spoke, and I am very glad to know that we can produce it at the reasonable cost of four cents each a year. That is much more reasonable than I thought. Is not this worth

while at such a small cost to ourselves, compared with what it must have cost those English villagers in centuries gone by to build their churches? Is it not worth while to do collectively these things which bring to us such satisfaction?
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these things are altogether consistent with all kinds of social amelioration. I do not see anything inconsistent between the production of public buildings and gardens and the emancipation of the people at large. I sometimes think the story of the alabaster box of ointment is altogether lost upon us. There were people in those days who said that this box could have been sold for much and given to the poor. That is an age-old argument. But the thing we want to get into our minds is that we ought to do this thing and not leave the other things undone, and I say that if we are true to our artistic and mental and moral ideals, if we seek to give our inward thought and feeling proper expression, the good time will more speedily come when justice and equality will spread from one ocean to the other.
So long as we choose to wallow in what is squalid and unsightly, I do not think we can ever find it in our hearts to make any widespread movement for social amelioration. I would be the last to discourage the spirit running through the Prime Minister's speech. On the contrary, I should like to see that spirit so developed that it would find expression not only in Ottawa but in every town and village throughout the Dominion. I want to see that spirit sustained so that in my little town at home it will find some form of expression. I do not want my children to go on living indefinitely in surroundings that are not worthy of a great country. I should like by co-operative or national methods to see the love of beauty inculcated in our people so that it would be manifested in their surroundings. I think I catch the right spirit in the speech of the Prime Minister, It seems to me that this young nation in the formative period of its history cannot afford to neglect those things which are sometimes stigmatized as impracticable. We, above all people, even at the cost of a little sacrifice, should see that future generations have something of an objective character by which to judge what we were mentally and morally.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we were all thrilled by the address of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and that we appreciate its sincerity and share his desire to see the capital of Canada so beautified as to attract the attention of the

world. For myself, I share in that sentiment without any qualification. But in the proposal before us and in the addresses of those advocating it what is chiefly dwelt upon is the "beautifying" of the city of Ottawa. I wonder if at this particular moment in our history we can spend a great deal of money on the simple element of "beauty." I have visited every legislative building in the Dominion. When in Halifax I was pleased to view the old door through which Joseph Howe used to slip at certain stages of the ceremonial of opening of the local house; I was glad to visit the old building in Charlottetown and to examine the table around which the fathers of confederation sat in 1865, and I derived a similar pleasure when going through the other legislative buildings throughout the Dominion. I have also visited the capitals of other countries, and I have observed that since 1914 no nation has spent much money on the beautification of its capital. The United States is spending no money in Washington to-day.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; They are spending fourteen million dollars on one bridge at this moment.

That may look a great deal to us, but what does it amount to in the United States? The government of the United States are turning their attention to something that they deem to be much more important, something that we should take cognizance of-the reduction of the nationaj debt. To-day the United States is almost out of debt; it has reduced its national debt from twenty-six billion to sixteen billion dollars-
They are almost out of debt.

-and eleven billion dollars of that is unloaded upon other countries. In another five or six years the people of the United States wild be absolutely relieved of their national debt. If, as a result of this, some of our people are moving across the line to-day in order to be relieved of some of the taxation incidental to our national debt, what will be the condition in this regard a few years hence when the national debt of the United States is no longer a burden in the shape of taxation?
Now, while I should like to see money spent in Ottawa, I have just one word to say to *he people of this city: There is a fundamental necessity in every community on the face of the earth which should be provided for, but it has not been provided for 'by this city-viz a supply of pure water.
Hear, hear.

As a Canadian I protest against the attitude of the city of Ottawa in regard to its water supply. This is an opportune time for parliament to say something in this regard. I know it is usual for men like the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) to smile when a question of this kind is mentioned, simply because they are not acquainted with the fundamental requirements of every progressive community. We should say to the city of Ottawa: Until you supply the city and the capital with .pure water, which is part of your municipal duty, we do not feel disposed to spend any more money in beautifying the city. I take that ground, Mr. Speaker, and I shall urge my views against propositions of this kind until' the city of Ottawa comes to its senses in this regard.
For a number of years we have been endeavouring to induce the city to provide a proper supply of water, but we have always met with obstruction. For one thing, the local newspapers take opposite views and raise all kinds of objections. To-day -the city of Ottawa is charging its people per capita less for water than is charged by any other city of its size on the continent of North America. If it were to charge a price equal to the average price obtaining on this continent, it oould provide a filtered, supply of water that would foe a credit to the city and be satisfactory to .those who have come here to attend to the business of the nation. As a member olf the provincial! board of health it was my duty, some ten or fifteen years ago, to study water conditions in this city. Sometimes we thought we were coming to a satisfactory conclusion, but difficulties would arise and nothing was accomplished. To-day the work of tire provincial board of health has been taken over by the provincial government and its functions are under the control of a member of the provincial cabinet-a circumstance which is weakening the bands of those who are trying to accomplish this improvement, because they are trying to make the question a semi-pdlitical issue. The government is afraid to urge the city of Ottawa to do its duty by itself and by the country for fear that some opposition may be reflected in the ballot box-not the unmarked ballots found on the street, but in, genuine ballots cast in the election of representatives in Ontario. Uniless members of parliament stand up at opportune times and voice their sentiments in this regard, urging the city of Ottawa to do its duty both by itself and by the city as the capital of this Dominion, I fear that

Now, Mr. Chairman, in the divorce courts which are established in the various provinces provision is made for alimony.

for.

'A provision then may be made-shall I alter that?-for alimony. It seems to me that the utmost care ought to be taken in regard to these cases, especially when children are concerned. I take it that the bringing of children into the world and their education is one of the fundamental principles of the family tie; yet we dissolve that tie without making any real protection for the children. I do not think that should any longer be permitted. We should decide definitely which of the two parents should have the custody of the children, and how these children are to be maintained. Even when there are not children, it seems to me that if a man is married to a woman and spends some years with her the least he can do where divorce is granted, especially where he himself is the guilty one, is to make some financial provision for her future. In one of the gases which is before us-I do not wish to enter into the details-there are three children involved. The man apparently has lived a very careless life; as a matter of faot he is at present in an institution and his family are dependent upon the help of friends.
I should like, to call attention to the fact that my suggestion is not an unknown thing or without precedent. I find that in the first divorce bill granted in Canada that was not referred to Great Britain, various provisions for the separation of the parties were made, and further there was provision for alimony, provision for the custody of the one child, and an allowance for the support of the child, with very adequate means for the enforcement of these requirements. There was also provision that in case of reconciliation between the husband and wife that the law should not come into force. It was said at the time that this was a matter that involved civil rights and hence did not come under the jurisdiction of the federal authorities. I anticipate that objection on this ground may be raised to an amendment which I may propose to-night-that this is a matter involving civil rights. But this

was the ground which was taken when the motion was finally passed in the house. I refer to the Campbell case of 1879, and I shall read just a paragraph from the statement made at that time by Senator Miller, as follows:
Under the British North America Act the legislation in regard to civil rights is given exclusively to the local legislatures, but it cannot be controverted, I think, that when the parliament of Canada has exclusive power to deal with any subject of legislation, that so far as it is_ necessary to deal with civil rights in connection with such legislation, we have the undoubted power to deal with them, where this parliament has the right to legislate on any subject it piust be considered that we have the power to legislate regarding all matters incident to that subject.
And then later on:
_ The whole legislative power, the whole functions of the government of this country have been remodelled anew, and under the British North America Act this question has been given absolutely to the control of this parliament.
And then again he saya:
Is it not, therefore, absurd to say that if we have the power by act of legislation to sweep out of existence the divorce courts of the provinces, and deprive them of all their authority respecting the subject of marriage and divorce, that we have not the power to deal with the whole subject and its incidents under the terms of the British North America Act? I think there cannot be very strong doubts that we have the power. Marriage and divorce, and everything which is incident to marriage and divorce, as a logical sequence and corollary, are within our jurisdiction. What then is alimony? It is maintenance after the separation of the husband and wife. It is an incident of the contract of marriage. So control of children is also a right growing out of the same contract; and. therefore, being incident to the marriage relationship, belongs to the jurisdiction of this parliament.
I may say that the house passed the bill without debate, the first instance of a divorce bill in Canada being passed without being reserved for his majesty. It is quite obvious that it is next to impossible for parliament to have a committee inquire info the details of the circumstances of each of the families concerned, but surely it is highly important that such an inquiry should be made. That is my reason for urging that we should transfer some of the powers originally held by parliament to a more suitable body which can safeguard the interests especially of the women and children.
But there is something more than that. There are a number of cases-and I want to be frank and say that this condition is not by any means universal-that come before the house this year in which the evidence shows that one or both of the people involved
are physically diseased. It seems to me that some day we shall reach the point where we shall insist that every man and' woman before marriage shall be able to give a clean bill of health; That should and must come in this country; but it has not yet come, and I suppose in the majority of cases we may take it for granted, unless something to the contrary arises, that the people are physically in good health. But there is in the hands of the members of this house evidence in printed form that some of these people are diseased. There is evidence in at least one case, and I hold in my hand a pamphlet of more than a hundred pages in which the evidence is given that the man has been addicted to the most horrible unnatural practices. I do not want just at this stage to have to connect the name with this, not only because of the man but particularly because of the; wife and child; but when we have cases in which there are the most horrible and unnatural practices, where the man is physically diseased and1 his wife is also physically diseased) and under treatment from a physician, it is the most absurd thing and it is morally indefensible for this house to grant the right to marry again. I do not think, in the interest of the future of this country that we should permit such a thing to occur. When a ease lake that arises I could hardly feel justified in saying that the man has a right to marry again. I suppose technically in the form in which the clause is worded, it is the woman who has the right to marry again, but I understand in practice the man has also that right. Thus we give him an opportunity of going out and ruining other lives as he has ruined the life of the woman who is now his wife. In such cases I should like to have the bill amended by adding the following words at the end of section 2, that is the section giving the right to marry again:
Provided that this right shall be exercised only upon condition that he shall be previously examined by competent medical authorities and pronounced free of venereal disease.
That seems to be a reasonable thing. I do not like to discuss these things; but if we condemn innocent people outside of this house to lives of misery-and I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who said the other day that there is tragedy in every one of these cases-we may well take our responsibilities a little more seriously than we have been doing. I am blaming myself along with the rest. Year after year I know I have protested against this procedure; but we all become absorbed in our business; things go as a matter of course, and we do not stop to consider all the consequences involved in

our votes. I will confess that I have read more of these cases in the last two or three days than I have read in the previous six or seven years. Most hon. members have hardly realized that there is no provision for the children, no provision for their education; that they are not even assigned to one or other of the parents. I know many hon. members do not realize the physical disabilities under which some of these people labour and the diseases with which they are afflicted, and these are matters that should be considered.
In view of that situation I do not think we are going too far when we urge that the government should offer facilities for the discussion of the bill that is now on the order paper. Last year a similar bill came from the senate and it received no discussion whatever. It came towards the close of parliament; there was no one to father it at that time, and possibly it would not have passed at that late date. This year again a similar bill comes over from the senate. The senators find it simply impossible to keep up with this work. I am informed that we have something like three hundred divorce bills that must be considered this year, or at least applications have been made for something like that number of divorces. I am also informed that altogether the senate cannot get through more than two hundred divorce cases and that something like seventy-five will go by the board this year. If we are anxious that these people should in some way settle down in their lives, surely it is highly desirable that we do not postpone for another twelve months the decision concerning their marital relations. We should decide and either force them to live together, if we can do that, or give them an opportunity of living apart. We should do that at this session.
We are facing this situation. This bill has come over from the senate in the ordinary course of affairs; it is down in the midst of public bills and orders, and it will hardly be reached this session. In the meantime we are carrying on along the old lines because apparently we have not the courage to break precedents and face the situation which ought to have been faced much earlier. In the earlier times we know that only the wealthy people came to parliament to secure divorces, and while I suppose it was as great a social evil in those days as it is to-day, certainly the numbers involved were not so great. I suppose in most cases then there could be arrangements made with regard to allocation of property; but now that large numbers of comparatively poor people are seeking divorces-

and in this province and in Quebec they have no other way of obtaining them than by coming to parliament-our procedure means that they are put to a great deal of unnecessary expense, inconvenience and an enormous amount of publicity that is far from being desirable. After that is all done in no one instance are we satisfactorily settling the case. We are allowing the children to be scattered abroad without making any provision for them. Therefore I would urge the Prime Minister under these circumstances to afford facilities this session for discussing this particular bill. I do not want to threaten as to what we may do; but it is quite obvious that even half a dozen members in this corner could obstruct to such an extent that we would indefinitely delay these bills so that they would not be passed this year and there would be even a greater public scandal; that we would force other bills to be delayed and thus again interfere with the business of parliament and of the country. It is not my desire nor the desire of anyone in this part of the chamber to do anything of that character, and we do not want anyone to think we are going to threaten to do it. But I appeal to the Prime Minister and the government to do what is the reasonable thing under the circumstances, namely, to give us an opportunity of considering the bill which is urged upon us by the senate, if necessary to vote it down, but in any case to consider what is to be done. Then another year, if we are to go forward in this haphazard fashion, some of us will be prepared perhaps to go to greater-extremes than we feel justified in doing at the present time.

I think the request of the hon. member for WetaSkiwin (Mr. Irvine) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), that the Prime Minister state whether he would give the house an opportunity of discussing Bill No. 27, is a reasonable one. Certainly this bill is introduced by a private member, yet it is a public bill that is all important, probably of more importance than anything else on the order paper. If this bill were passed' by the house it would make a very great deal of difference in the transaction of the business of this house in future sessions. This bill passed the senate this year at an early stage of the session. We have sometimes heard very hard things said about hon. members sitting in another chamber. They have rejected bills of ours because they have not had time to consider them towards the end of the session. Here is a case where a bill came from that chamber very early in the session, and has been before us for some time. I think it is only reasonable that the house should be given an opportunity to discuss it.

My only reason for rising to say a few words at this time is to emphasize the injustice that is done to private members under the rules as they exist to-day. Here we have under the heading of public bills and orders no less than seventeen different bills and resolutions. All these measures have been introduced and partly discussed, and they are all now buried under public bills and orders, which appears to be simply a graveyard for private members'' bills and resolutions. It does seem to me that if a private member is allowed to introduce a bill or resolution he should also be allowed to bring it before the house in such a way that parliament can make a decision upon it. What I am protesting against is that while all these measures are of importance to the members concerned, and of importance also to their constituents and to many people in the country, yet under the
rules parliament is prevented from coming to a decision upon them. Surely nothing could be fairer than that an opportunity should be afforded for finishing the discussion that has already begun on these questions and having a vote upon them.
It appears to me that under the present rules too much power entirely is centralized in that section of parliament which is called the government. The rest of the house has apparently little or no power; we are hampered in so many different ways. For instance, any bill or resolution involving the expenditure of ihoney cannot be brought before the house by a private member, and any other measure not involving the expenditure of money which a private member does bring forward can very conveniently be buried among -public bills and orders.
I am not prepared to say whether or not I am in favour of bill No. 27. I have not given it very much consideration. I am not demanding that the bill be passed. I am simply asking that parliament in the ordinary course of events be given an opportunity to pass its opinion on that bill. The rules are very remarkable when a few members of the house can obstruct business in this way. I am going to be quite frank and say that, so far as I am concerned, I think the obstructionist tactics are quite justified. These rules seem to have been framed deliberately to prevent discussion and to prevent parliament from coming to a decision on matters brought before this house by a private member. The rules are framed to centralize power in that section of parliament which is called the government-
I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, to rule whether the hon. gentleman is in order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member who
has just taken his seat (Mr. Campbell) has said that the rules of the house had been so framed as to give private members no opportunity whatever to discuss bills or resolutions introduced by them, and to put the control of business into the hands of the government. May I remind him that the rules of the house to which he refers are the result of a conference which took place between all parties in this house, including the party of which he himself is a member, and the report which was brought into this house with regard to the new rules was passed unanimously, my hon. friend himself being one of those who concurred in it. So that as far as the rules under which we are working at the moment are concerned, every hon. member of this house was a consenting party to them. The rules were adopted unanimously. If there are difficulties in the working out of those rules, that possibly is to be expected, but I submit that these difficulties will not be solved by adopting methods which really preclude free discussion, but rather by taking full advantage of the opportunities which the rules themselves permit.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite are interested in reaching a particular bill. The rules provide that on Tuesday and Friday evenings for the first hour private bills shall be the first order of business, and that private bills shall be succeeded by public bills. If the private bills are disposed of, we will then reach public bills, and I submit that the quickest way to reach the particular bill in which the hon. member is interested is to get the private bills out of the way so that we can come to order No. 31 for the second reading of the bill in which the hon. member is interested.
An appeal has been made to the government, and to myself in particular, to undertake ^ bo say that a certain public bill shall be given precedence anid preference over all other measures. There are at least a dozen members of the house who have made a similar appeal to me, not publicly, but privately, asking that preference be given to the particular bill in which they were specially interested. I have pointed out to one and all that to give preference to any single

measure was to work an injustice to all other hon. members who had private or public bills in which they were specially interested. For that reason I have refused to comply with their request.
Is not a senate bill in a somewhat different class?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All private bills are private bills whether they originate in this or in the other house.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall that two or three days ago I made a motion in the house, and I think it was out of that motion that the present discussion has in part arisen, to get certain senate bills out of the way, so that other private bills could be brought on more speedily. Some hon. members took exception to that' motion, and the discussion that has been taking place ever since has really grown out of an endeavour on the part of the government to expedite these senate measures with a view to enabling other private bills to be more speedily reached.
Could the Prime Minister not have just as reasonably and just as readily included this bill No. 27 in his motion, or made a similar motion referring to that bill only?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I again
point out to my hon. friend that, assuming the government wished to take a particular bill and have it considered, the final decision as to whether or not the bill can be dealt with out of the order prescribed by the rules of the house rests with the house itself, not with the government. I submit that unless there is an obvious disposition on the part of members in all parts of the house to endeavour to facilitate and expedite the business with respect to private bills, any appeal on the part of the government to give preference to a particular bill just because one section of the house is interested in it would not meet with the approval which those most interested wish to have. I suggest that we make an effort to take up these private bills in as expeditious a manner as possible. The government recognizes there are some important measures that hon. members will wish to have considered, and it may be that a little later on in the session the government will find it advisable to grant a special time for further consideration of private bills, but it must be a consideration that applies equally to all bills and not to any one bill in particular.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 218, to amend the Federal District Commission Act, 1927.

Federal District-Mr. McGibbon

Before this bill passes there are one or two observations I wish to make. I listened this afternoon with considerable interest to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and that of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), and I fancy that nearly every hon. member in this house and everyone in the country will agree that this capital should be beautified. We are all interested in this matter, just as we are interested in our individual municipalities and in our own homes and everything appertaining thereto. But, Mr. Speaker, there is something else that must be considered, and that is the advisability of this parliament voting so much money at the present time for an object of this character. The first essential which this parliament should consider is that the government that raises money by taxation must be held responsible for spending it. That principle has been violated by this government on many occasions this session. Of course, we have always been given reasons. The Prime Minister this afternoon addressed the house for an hour explaining why this expenditure should be made at the present time. In all my public or private career I have never known of a government, a municipality or a person spending money belonging to someone else who could not find excuses for so doing, but I have found it much more difficult to find people who practise economy and handle public funds as they should be handled. Here we are voting $3,000,000 to put so many buildings into the scrap heap- I was going to say it would be squandered, but possibly that is too strong. At any rate we are spending $3,000,000 and in addition we are voting $200,000 a year for thirty years, making $6,000,000 more.
This afternoon the Prime Minister cited the United States as an example, but I should like to ask him Whether the financial condition of this country to-day is comparable to that of the United States. Does he think this country has made such progress financially since the war as would enable it to imitate the United States? This afternoon the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) drew attention to a fact of which I do not think sufficient notice has been taken by parliament and the country. He told us that the government of the United States have reduced the national debt of that country from twenty-six billion to about sixteen billion dollars, and have reduced taxes from $50 to $25 per head. In addition to that, of the sixteen billion dollars remaining of their national debt, they have unloaded between
eleven and twelve billion dollars on Great Britain and other countries. If they continue their present rate of progress, paying a billion dollars a year, in five years they will be free of war taxation. Consequently we see that they are in a much better position than the Dominion of Canada to undertake obligations of this kind.
I object to this expenditure for another reason; the people in the rural municipalities of the province of Ontario get practically nothing from this government. For example, in my riding there are many localities which receive only two deliveries of mail a week, and when we ask the department for something more they tdll us the business will not warrant it. I would also point out that the mail service is practically the only thing given by the government to the ordinary resident in a rural municipality.

I should like to say just a word on the question of mail service. No request has been received within the last eighteen months from any part of Canada asking for more than two mails a week which has not been granted. I wish to have that statement corrected.
Then I would ask the Postmaster General a further question. If such requests come in will he grant them?

I will, because generally
speaking, I do not consider two mails a week sufficient for any part of this country where post offices are established.

I am very glad I rose to-night, if for no other reason than that I have secured this promise from the Postmaster General. I have gone to his department, although not to him personally, to ask for this service, and have been told that the business would not warrant it. I am very grateful, therefore, to the Postmaster General for this promise, and I can assure him that before many days pass he will receive such a request from at least one riding.
There is another point to which I would like to direct the attention of the Prime Minister and the government, a point which I am glad to say was touched upon by the Prime Minister this afternoon. I refer to the creation of Ottawa as a federal district. While we are tearing down the Russell house at a cost of $1,250,000 in order to beautify this city, a structure is going up on Wellington street right in front of the parliament buildings which at this stage appears to have no architectural beauty at all. I suggest to the Prime Minister and the government that this should be created a federal district in the near future in order that the government may have some
