control over all buildings erected within a certain distance of the parliament buildings. As things now stand, I can see no sense in tearing down a building such as the Russell house because it is an eyesore situated near the parliament buildings, white another building is going up much closer which probably will not be so beautiful.
There are many things which I believe are needed by the country more than what this expenditure is being made for. The Postmaster General has promised a better mail service, and now I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) if he will carry out the intention of parliament as expressed a few years ago in regard to relief for Home bank depositors. A number of people lost their money in that institution. I am not going to discuss the question whether the government were right or wrong in granting them 35 per cent of their losses, but I do say that since that principle was adopted everyone should be treated alike. Up to the present some have received 35 per cent, but because the money ran out others whose claims were admitted received only 25 per cent, 20 per cent, 15 per cent, and in some cases only 10 per cent. As I have said, there might have been some justification for parliament not giving anything, but I can see no justice in a discrimination of this kind. I ask the Minister of Finance if he will not treat all alike and do justice to everyone. I hope he will be as frank as the Postmaster General, so I will pause for a reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look
at Hansard to-morrow morning he will find that I made a statement on the orders of the day this afternoon with regard to the Home bank.

I heard the statement
made by the minister, but it does not cover what I am asking now. He said then he would grant their claims at least in part, but I do not see how the government can discriminate between these people. I agree that at that time the government had a good argument for not doing anything. I was not in the house then so I do not take any responsibility one way or the other, but there were two sides to the question and Hansard of that time shows that a very good case was presented on the floor of this house for both sides. However, parliament having decided that the government should grant 35 per cent, first to all depositors having under 1500 in that bank and then to all those who had over $500 in the bank and could prove that they were in need of it, and the Exchequer Court having 
decided who were in need of it, I cannot see why there should be any discrimination and why some should be paid 35 per cent while others receive as little as 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow
me to say a word just to keep the record straight, the measure which was passed by this chamber at the instance of the government provided for something over $5,000,000, which would have taken care of everyone on the basis just outlined by my hon. friend. That bill was amended in the other chamber, however, and the amendment was accepted by this house.

I am quite familiar with that fact. I believe an estimate was called for as to how much money would be required to care for these people, but after all it was only an estimate and because it was below actual requirements I do not see that that is any occasion for doing an injustice. However, I believe the minister is honest enough to see that this is not working out fairly and I believe he will yet remedy the situation, because I do not believe any honest man can justify a discrimination of that kind. If we have millions to spend: if we can hand over seven millions as we did the other night to the Quebec harbour commission and $700,000 to Toronto, and if we can vote millions here for the destruction of buildings in Ottawa, surely we can do justice to those who have lost their all and have got beyond the stage in life where they can earn a living and are depending upon this money. My last appeal to the Prime Minister and the government is to equalize the task which they have undertaken and to do justice to all these people.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express the pleasure I experienced in hearing the right hon. the Prime Minister this evening give reasons why the national capital should be placed under some definite scheme of improvement. I was very much impressed with the pictures that were drawn of the various capitals in Europe and on the North American continent, and I felt mysel'f in accord with all that the Prime Minister said. But when he had finished I thought this an opportune moment to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister and the government a different aspect of the question, a different picture, so that a due sense of proportion might be brought into action with regard to Canada as a whole.
Centralization of investment and improvement was never a part of the confederation scheme, and much, sir, as I appreciate and realize the necessity of the beautification of

Federal District-Mr. Brady
our capital city; much as I admire what has been done here in respect to the victory tower and the perpetuation therein for future generations of the story of the brave deeds of our 50,000 Canadians, still I feel that I should not be doing right if, as the representative of a courageous and hardworking people,
I did not present their view in the hope that the same spirit of generosity with which we are now going to vote $6,000,000 covering a period of thirty years and $3,000,000 for immediate use, may be accorded them, I am sure the ministers of every department of the government must be tired reading the letters of hon. members pleading for a little wharf here, a little marine light there, a telephone line to some community for women and children removed from the centres of civilization. But when I find, sir, that sometimes we cannot get even a hundred dollars, -a small amount, but it means a big thing to the people affected-I ask the Prime Minister and his government, not perhaps that they should go out of their way, but that they at least be actuated by the same spirit of generosity in relation to the people who need a little help, who are far removed from the parks and the squares and the boulevards but who are toiling hard to build up by their industry our great seaports and our cities; that they should give at any rate some consideration to the demands of these people.
I do not wish to dwell at length, Mr. Speaker, upon the side of our Canadian life which is often overlooked in this House of Commons. I have travelled not hundreds but thousands of miles through my constituency since last year; I have toiled and walked where roads do not exist, and I now plead for better care and a more sympathetic hearing for the people who are not capable of coming to the House of Commons to plead their own case. There are districts where women and children live with no doctors within often thirty miles, and no telephone communication. That is not confined merely to one part of western Canada; it- is a condition which is very general. I have pleaded in this house, sir, for twelve months for fishermen's floats, which are necessary to the safeguarding of the whole of their interests, their capital, their homes, because all these are centred in their boats; but a. deaf ear has been turned to the plea of the people.
I wish to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a grave duty incumbent upon a government. They are placed in power for a limited period, to do, not for a section but for the good of the whole, that which ought to be done. I assure the hon. Prime Minister that members on this side of the house
are not chronic in their opposition to government measures; they give the deepest consideration to them, and they are ever ready to support measures which are in the national interest. But I say that in the matter of public works, in the matter of the assistance to the people who are building up this country, the government are not carrying out that duty which they should take upon themselves as a sacred pledge to perform. After this matter has been thoroughly threshed out, therefore, I trust that if the representatives of the people of Canada are in accord with the beautification of their capital city, rural interests will not suffer and a response will be made to our requests in this house for the very things which will enable Canada at a crucial moment of her existence to keep her people on the land, to keep them in the vocations for which they are best fitted, and not cause them to be driven daily into our cities with resulting unemployment and such scenes as have been witnessed in Winnipeg in the last few days. The greatest scheme of immigration, sir, that Canada can put into force is the taking of such action as may be necessary to assist our people who are now on the land and who are willing to stay there and whose children would live with them and build up the country if they were given the little help for which they ask. I have placed before the ministers here communications not from one person but boards of trade, representing whole communities, some of them large districts, begging for a few hundred dollars for a wharf upon a lakeside which would enable those people to avoid a journey of thirty or forty miles along very poor roads. And what has been the answer? The answer has very often been a polite little note, very often of three lines, that the matter will be looked into. That is all we get and we have to go back with that to our constituents. The hour is coming when the people of Canada will realize that it is not politics they want, but men who are pledged, irrespective of localitiy or of political feelings, to do what is right for the people as a whole.
I am in sympathy with the scheme of beautifying Ottawa. In my young days I was favoured with the opportunity of travelling throughout Europe and I know the heritage that a great country can store up for future generations in its buildings, museums, libraries and art galleries. All these are necessary for the life, spirit and growth.of a nation; but the large sums of money spent in certain localities in Canada are out of all due proportion to their needs, while large parts of this country are left outside in the cold, pleading in vain for trade facilities. That is exactly why I

Federal District-Mr. Coote
stand here to-night representing those people I am doing it not as a politician but with a heart as pure, with motives as sincere and with aspirations as great as those of any member on the government side.
When the Prime Minister this afternnon displayed that eloquence of his in support of his measure, I thought for a moment perhaps he was ignorant of another picture on a bigger and broader scale, a picture not of a city but of a vast stretch of country awaiting a little help. It is only a little-a bagatelle when you consider the expenditure of $250,000 a year for thirty years. I thought if only the Department of Public Works, the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the other departments would give even an amount equivalent to a small fraction of that, we would be helping to make a contented, happy people. Canadians love their land. They would like to live there always. We have a great fertile country, millions of acres yet unsettled, and what is happening? People who have spent the best part of their lives in trying to make a living in the country by farming, give up in despair. Who would not under similar conditions? Therefore I appeal this evening to the representatives of Quebec, the oldest and most prosperous province in Canada, that they should treat matters such as we are discussing here to-night on the big, broad basis that what is good for British Columbia, must be good for Canada; for the development of western Canada will, benefit eastern Canada as well. I am not an expert in financial matters; I am not an expert in the business world; but at least I have a knowledge of the history of the past and the present trend of modern life, and, I aver the day will come when Canada will regret that she did not in the golden opportunity of her youth do more to keep our people on the land and build up healthy prosperous rural communities. We are sadly neglecting this important duty today. So far as I have been able I have done my duty. I care a great deal about the future of young Canadian people; I feel deeply for the thousands who are now struggling against difficulties which the government have it in their power to remedy.
In conclusion, let me say that this session of parliament has been an anxious one to many of our members. We found that it was not safe during the winter months for any member leaving the parliament buildings alone to proceed on any of the walks other than that leading directly to the main entrance. Why? He might slip, as many have slipped, on one of the sidewalks and, if hurt, be left lying there the whole night long and probably

lose his life. The way the walks to and about the parliament buildings have been kept this winter was a disgrace, and a bounden duty rests upon the government to see that in future the place is at least made safe for pedestrians.
Another matter I should like to speak of is in reference to the water used for drinking purposes, but I am not going to blame the government for it. I have travelled a good deal in my life I have never tasted worse water than that of the city of Ottawa. The other day in my private home where I live the landlady placed water on my table for luncheon and she said:	"Do not worry about
the water, I have placed something in it."
Oh, oh.

It was nothing except some purifying agent. Why was that done? It was done because the water was so muddy that no one could drink it. I should like the Prime Minister now that he is sponsoring a special scheme providing for the beautification of the city of Ottawa, to exert his power and influence to see to it that the other part, namely, a better water supply and the cleaning up of the city so as to keep pace with the beautification scheme proposed by the Prime Minister, be given the necessary attention.

I wish to take just a few minutes of the time of the house before this bill goes into the committee stage on account of remarks which were made by the Prime Minister this afternoon in reference to the statement that I had made a year ago. I have taken the trouble to look up Hansard of last year, and it may be recalled that I pointed out then that one thing which in my opinion should be done by the Ottawa improvement commisison, with the assistance of the government, was to secure the property on Wellington street between Metcalfe and O'Connor-that is the section immediately facing the parliament buildings 

that an open space should be provided there extending at least from the grounds of the parliament buildings down to Sparks street, and that on the remainder of the block buildings be erected which would harmonize with the architectural design of the parliament buildings. Since that time a new building has been started on the corner of O'Connor and Wellington streets, so that we are a year too late in regard to that project. I can only express my regret that the government did not first of all secure this property immediately facing the parliament buildings and proceed to beautify it.

Federal District-M r. Geary
The capital of Canada centres on what we call parliament hill. This is the spot from which we should start to beautify the capital. I am afraid the proposal which is contained in this bill to add one more park to the city of Ottawa, while that is very desirable if we can afford it, is not the step which should have been taken first. If this is all the money we can afford to spend-and I take it from the discussion here to-day that that is the way parliament feels about it- I regret that the money was not used in securing the property on Wellington street directly in front of the parliament buildings, and then starting from the very centre of the capital to beautify it. Any further suggestions or criticisms that I may have to make, Mr. Speaker, I shall postpone until the bill is in committee.

Before the Prime Minister replies would he allow me to ask him a question? When the plans were adopted and parliament voted 8250,000 a year for sixteen years, it seems to me that the commission must have had in view at that time the plaza or open space which is shown on the chart that has been distributed to-day. If so, the commission must have had also in its mind that something should be done with the Russell house block. Whether they contemplated leaving the Russell house standing or acquiring it and doing something with it, may be a matter of question, but in either case one would think they must have had the situation in mind when they were asking for $250,000 for sixteen years. If, on the other hand, the purchase of the Russell house block is a new development, I should like the Prime Minister to indicate that to the house when he is replying.

I would like to point out just one or two features in connection with this important bill. I believe when the Prime Minister introduced the bill he made mention of the fact that we should look forward to Ottawa becoming a federal district, and that that ideal would be nearer of attainment after another redistribution measure was before the house. I think our last census was taken in 1921, so the next will be in 1931. A redistribution measure will be due shortly after the census which is to be taken in 1931, and in view of that fact I was wondering if there is any real need at this time for this legislation which is now proposed. Last session we had brought before us a bill providing for an appropriation of a quarter of a million dollars for each of the next succeeding sixteen years for the federal 56103-149
district commission. It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that that provision would amply take care of the needs of the commission for such time as will elapse between now and the next redistribution bill, and would it perhaps not be tJhe part of wisdom on the part of this house to go gently along as we are doing, and then make a thorough j ob of the business after the next redistribution?
It seems to me that we are starting in even on this measure a quarter of a century too late. I think there is more in this city that needs renovating than just the driveways and parks. It is true that it is very pleasant to take a drive over a splendid driveway and to refresh yourself in a most beautiful park, but you forget all that pleasantness if you take a walk along Bank street about five in the afternoon. You are badgered from pillar to post, you trip over water hydrants, and are jostled by pedestrians, so that at times it is certainly not pleasant travelling along Bank street. If this city were under the administration of a commission and the territory turned into a federal district, such a thing as the widening of Bank street and making it more fit for pedestrians might be attended to.
It has also been mentioned here that Wellington street is hardly safe to cross. I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that we are going to continue as we are in that respect until there is a casualty on Wellington street, and then we will seriously consider the situation. Every day, on crossing that street, those of us who are so unfortunate as to have to cross it on foot have to dodge cars coming and going not at any fifteen or twenty miles an hour, but from thirty to fifty miles an hour, and the marvel is to me that we have not had casualties ere this. I do not know who has authority to supervise that situation. I believe that a part of Wellington street is under the control of the federal government, and that another part is under the control of the city, but if the whole street were under a federal commission, and the whole city were turned into a federal district, that situation could easily be taken care of.
Another matter that might be beneficial would be taking care of the civil service. If the city were turned into a federal district, I presume that the civil service would be disfranchised. Possibly that might not necessarily be entailed in such a procedure, but it would seem to me a very wise step to take. Then there would not be a continual bombardment not only of the members representing the city of Ottawa, but of other hon. members with a view to positions in the civil service, the reviewing of salaries, and such like.

The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) mentioned that this expenditure was so trivial that it amounted to only four cents per capita per year. That may be true in regard to this particular expenditure, but the trouble is we have so many of these trivial expenditures. We have $8,500,000 for Quebec harbour, $5,000,000 for St. John harbour, and $500,000 for another harbour, etcetera, etcetera,_ and we have hanging over our head a national debt of almost two and a half billion dollars, which amounts to almost $300 per capita. So it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are going rather extravagantly, to put it mildly, and that we can well afford to let at least this measure of extravagance ride over for a. few years. If we have another census in 1031, that is only a matter of three years, and a redistribution bill will be brought down shortly after that. In from three to five years we could perhaps have a federal district created here, and the commissioners in charge could build from the ground up and create a capital city which would be of real beauty and of which the nation might well be proud.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express on behalf of the government, my appreciation of the manner in which the proposal that I made has on the whole been received by hon. members. It was perhaps too much to expect that an opportunity would not be taken to point out wherein an equivalent expenditure might serve an infinite variety of needs in different parts of the country and particularly in the constituencies of hon. members. But I would say in respect of any requests that have been made to the government for consideration, if any can be found which promise to be an equally good investment on the part of the nation, I think the government will be ready favourably to consider them. What has possibly escaped the attention of some who have been critical is the fact that the government is not giving away this money. We are purchasing property which will be owned by the Dominion of Canada, and which will enhance in value very greatly as the years go by. A parallel case may be suggested. When parliament hill and the properties in the immediate vicinity were purchased some years ago, no doubt there were many who felt that the money then being expended on this wide-open space might more properly be devoted to a variety of other purposes. But who would say to-day that the investment had not in the course of the years multiplied itself many times over?
I Mr. Carmichael.]

May I interrupt the
right hon. gentleman to remark that as I understand it this land is to become the property of the federal district commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The federal
district commission is created by the government for the purpose of administering the-property, but the property will belong to the people of Canada. I venture to say that in the course of the thirty years which has been mentioned as the time over which expenditures might be made, this property will have paid for itself time and time over in the mere appreciation of value that will have taken place. On a cash basis therefore, if we are to measure it in terms of money pure and simple, the government is really making an investment of very considerable value to the nation, and if one were seeking further justification; it might well be looked for from that point of view.
May I say a word in regard to what has been expressed by hon. gentlemen opposite as to there being in this particular measure some evasion of the principle of responsible government? There is no such evasion in what the government is proposing. There is no seeking to get away in any particular from the control of parliament. At this very moment parliament is giving all the powers that can possibly be given under this legislation. No power will be given to any commission or to any executive or to any body-other than what this parliament gives at this particular time. Every dollar to foe expended will be a dollar that this parliament has voted and is appropriating by assenting to this legislation. That is responsible government in the fullest meaning of the term.
Further, I may add that all expenditures by the commission in the nature of capital expenditures have to be submitted to the Minister of Finance in the first instance and then approved by the government. The commission is the body entrusted with giving special thought and -attention as to what should be done, but every step has to be approved in the first instance by the government as a whole. So we are not turning over to parties who are in no way responsible to parliament sums of money to be expended as they may think fit. Moreover, the commission makes its report to parliament every year. One hon. member this afternoon had in his hand -a re' port made some years ago, and he said it was the last he was able to obtain. I might say to him that I have a report dealing with the proceedings of the commission fox the past

Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
year. It was tabled here only a short time ago by the Minister of Finance. Every year these reports are tabled.
With respect to expenditures, I would point out that the accounts of the commission may be examined by a committee of this parliament at any time. Some hon. member suggested that possibly the expenditures should come before the public accounts committee. Most decidedly they will come before the public accounts committee if there is the slightest reason to suspect that every dollar cannot-be accounted for in the fullest measure. The expenditures are audited by the Auditor General. This officer in that particular exercises the same control over the expenditures of the commission as over other expenditures by departments of government.

I am thoroughly familiar with the Audit Act, and I think the Prime Minister will find that unless special provision is made for the purpose neither the Auditor General nor a committee of the house has any control over the commission's expenditures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The act provides as follows:
The commission shall from time to time before making expenditures under this act, submit to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General detailed estimates of the expenditures proposed to be made by it, which estimates shall be accompanied by such full information as is sufficient to enable the governor in council to determine as to the necessity or advisability of such proposed expenditures, or of any portion thereof; and no expenditure shall be made by the commission under this act until it has been approved by the governor in council.
The commission shall send to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General on or before the first day of September in each year a detailed statement of all its receipts and expenditures up to the last day of March in such year; and copies of such statements shall be laid before parliament by the minister within the first fourteen days of the next following session thereof.
The commission shall, whenever required by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, render detailed accounts of its receipts and expenditures for such period or to such day as he designates; and all books of account, records, bank books and papers of the commission shall at all times be open to the inspection of the minister or of such person as the minister names to inspect them.
All expenditures by the commission shall be subject to the audit of the Auditor General in the same manner as other public moneys.

The point I desire to
make is that while the reports have to be made to the Minister of Finance and laid on the table, they are not subject to reference to the public accounts committee as are the reports of the Auditor General. If the Prime Minister makes that clear I shall be 56103-149^
abundantly satisfied with respect to it. Parliament should have this jurisdiction. In the one case it depends on the Minister of Finance whether the report goes to the public accounts committee; in the other it goes there as a matter of right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The public
accounts are laid on the table each year and referred by the Minister of Finance to the public accounts committee. With respect to these accounts, if any hon. member at any time wishes to have them so referred, the government will see that this is done.
That is very satisfactory.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think that
makes it clear that so far as the public money which we are voting is concerned, it is in every particular safeguarded by every means that parliament has devised for safeguarding the expenditure of public funds.
A good deal has been said about what the government is doing for the city. I was glad that the hon. leader of the opposition agreed with me that the distinction between Ottawa as the capital and Ottawa as a municipality should be kept in mind. From the city's point of view I may say that the argument is not all on the side of the government. The government has a large amount of . property in the city, and that property is exempt from taxation. I have been given *he following figures, which I assume may be taken as reliable. They are to the effect that in 1923-that is the latest year for which I could get them-the value of Dominion government property in Ottawa exempt from municipal taxation was $33,413,025. The present tax rate of the city is 31.70 mills. That is the annual rate that would be paid to the city on government property were it taxed like other property.

It is unnecessary to say
to the Prime Minister that the tax rate would go down at least half, because a million dollars bears such a proportion to the total revenue that the rate would at once decline.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am prepared to admit that this statement must be read in the light of economic considerations which would govern, but I am pointing out a truth which has more or less escaped attention during discussion, namely, that the city of Ottawa does not receive on government property any taxation, and that all it receives in lieu of taxation is an annual grant of $100,000. In 1924, in a memorandum submitted by the city of Ottawa, it was con-

Federal District-Mr. Mackenzie King
tended that the government should pay annually certain sums which I shall state. 1 am giving the city's contention; I am not saying that if it were examined, it would be upheld to the degree to which the city alleges it should be. These are the amounts: a grant of say, $100,000, towards the maintenance of a fire brigade, and of $40,000, towards the maintenance of the police department; towards pavements, streets and sewer maintenance, $50,000; towards street lighting, $5,000. These amounts total $105,000 and, if the government were in the same position in respect of its properties as the owners of other property in the city, these it is alleged would be the grants we would have to consider making, to some extent at least, to the city. In addition to the $100,000 in lieu of taxation, we pay, I understand, some $40,000 for a water supply, and that is all the city gets. When we consider the relations between the government and the city, I submit that the extra amount being given by the government to the city for improvement and park purposes may be regarded as certainly not in excess of an equivalent.
Now what is the exact extent of the present proposed outlay? A good deal has been said about the expenditure of millions. I have asked the Finance department to prepare a careful statement showing what an annual allowance of $200,000 over a period of thirty ' years, plus this capital investment of $3,000,000 extended over thirty years, would amount to per annum, and I am advised that, with borrowing powers at four and a half per cent on a thirty year basis, the capital outlay of $3,000,000, with an annual grant of $200,000, would represent an annual outlay of $384,200. That is the extent of what parliament is being asked at the moment to grant for the purpose of further improvements and maintaining the work that has already been undertaken. I believe the house will feel that this amount, taking all the circumstances into consideration, is a reasonable grant to the federal district commission.
Further, in speaking of the city and its obligations, I may say that I agree heartily with hon. members who have criticized the city for the water supply and the manner in which snow has been cleared. In discussing these matters with the city, I told the mayor very frankly that I should hesitate to come to parliament and ask for this appropriation unless I could get from him a direct assurance that the city intended to improve its water supply and its method of street cleaning. The mayor advises me that with respect to the water supply the board of control is at the

present time giving very serious consideration to this important question with a view to seeing what can best be done to improve matters and provide a purer supply of water.
Are they any more serious now than they were twenty years ago?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is something which my hon, friend will have to find out for himself. I cannot speak on behalf of the city council beyond expressing the belief that they are more serious. I imagine that, for one thing, public opinion in this city compels them to 'be more serious; and I believe that the many expressions of opinion that have come from parliament hill are not without their influence. Certainly unless the city in the matter of a pure water supply does waken up to its responsibilities to the citizens generally as well as to hon. members of this parliament, it will wait a long time before meeting with any sort of reception to a request for further co-operation on the part of the government. Not only must the city take the question of its water supply very seriously into consideration, but it must within a short time show us that it has found a means of providing such a supply of pure water as this city should have. With regard to the manner in which the streets have been cleaned, I am advised that the city has already undertaken to purchase equipment which, in another winter, will facilitate the plowing of 100 miles instead of 25 miles as has been the case up to the present time. They expect to have a much more effective means of dealing with the streets as respects the removal of snow.
As regards Wellington street in front of the parliament buildings, the government has directed attention repeatedly to what 'has appeared to be an abuse in permitting motors to be parked before the grounds of these buildings. We have also discussed the practice of rapid driving to and fro to the risk of pedestrians crossing Wellington street. Wellington street is controlled by the city and not by the government, and I am informed that the city7- council 'has passed an ordinance prohibiting parking on Wellington street in front of the parliament buildings. This regulation will be carried into force. The mayor, as recently as yesterday, assured me that this would be done, and asked for the co-operation of our own Department of Public Works in the matter. This I consider all-important: Wellington street should be kept free from parking, at least in front of these buildings and grounds.

I might say
to my hon. friend that a redistribution could not aifect the method of financing a project

Federal District Commission
such as the construction of driveways, park improvements and so on. That would have to be carried on under a federal district commission just as it is carried on now. The reason we are asking for a longer period of time is that it provides a guarantee of permanency and maintenance with respect to improvements which are to be made. It does give to the commission for a few years some small margin to work on in the matter of local improvements, although it is contemplated that by the end of thirty years the full amount of $200,000 will be required solely for purposes of maintenance. At present I understand that half of the original grant, which would be something like $125,000 a year, is required for the actual upkeep of the parks and the overhead expenses of what had been previously provided for.

I suggest to the government the desirability of substituting the word "five" for the word "thirty". Five years is the life of a parliament, and I cannot think it quite consonant with the ideas of the right hon. gentleman as heretofore expressed that this parlianient should bind the hands of future parliaments. I am quite aware of the fact that it would be quite competent for succeeding parliaments to change that figure to forty or to ten; they would have that power, but a vested interest is acquired when a statute of this kind is passed by parliament; the commission naturally expects that that is the end of it. I suggest that instead of making provision for thirty years we endeavour to deal with this matter during the lifetime of a parliament. It is true that one or two sessions of this parliament will have passed, but I think the right hon. gentleman would be quite within the general constitutional practice if he said, "I desire that a given sum shall be available for this commission during the lifetime of the parliament over which I am the directing head." But when you ask parliament to bind its hands for thirty years I cannot help but think that is going too far, and that it is not quite consistent with the general principles under which we conduct our government.
I made inquiries to-day of my hon. friend from Welland as to the practice followed by the Ontario commission, and the house has already heard me state the facts as they apply there. -Every year they bring up their estimates; although frequently they have made provision for five year periods or even longer, each year the legislature votes the sum of money which may be required to give effect to the projected plans of the commission. Having regard to the fact that this legislation is
'Mr. Mackenzie King.]
practically but an amendment to the Federal District Commission Act which was passed last year, and having regard to the fact that the Minister of Finance must review the expenditures and the governor in council must pass upon them, I cannot but think this mere declaration that $200,000 should be made available should not be binding for more than the life of a parliament as established by statute, which is five years. Assuming there was an election at the end of four years resulting in the defeat of the administration, as has happened in this country, the estimates for the fifth year might be fairly thought to be within the competence of the outgoing administration as far as the commission is concerned.
In order that the matter may be considered by the committee in a concrete way, I move that the word "thirty" be struck out and the word " five " substituted therefor, for the reasons I have indicated.

If the Prime Minister is prepared to go so far as to say that while it is not part of the present scheme it is in contemplation and will certainly result, in perhaps three or four years, in the removal of the post office, perhaps we would support that part of the proposition. But that does not appear to be part of the scheme; it is not in contemplation, and therefore I think the proposed expenditure is an extravagance. A driveway which would complete the drive from the experimental farm to Rockliffe, is, I think, very necessary. I have seen many driveways but I have never seen any city which has a more beautiful driveway than has Ottawa. As far as spending money upon that is concerned,
I am in favour of ilt; and there should be a connection between that, driveway from where it now enters under Laurier Avenue to a point near the Chateau. I can quite understand that it might be thought necessary to have a driveway starting from somewhere near the drill hall and gradually rising to reach the square in front of the buildings, and this plan of course contemplates that, but it contemplates such a driveway going through the land on which the Russell block now stands. Whalt is the necessity for that? I do not think it is any compliment to the edity of Ottawa, with a population of 125,000 or 130,000 people, that from a commercial, industrial and business standpoint you can pull down one of the best blocks on the most important corner in the heart of the city at- a cost of SI,250,000, merely to make a park. I do not know whether or not the citizens of Ottawa are in favour of such a scheme; I Can hardly imagine they would be, Where can you find on the continent of America a city that would want to have one of its 'best blocks in the very heart of it pulled down merely to make a park about two hundred feet square? If you could not get an entrance to the parliament grounds without doing this there might be some justification for it.
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
I agree with the Prime Minister that if a large sum of money is to be spent, the proper place to spend it would be in widening Metcalfe street perhaps as far as Laurier avenue so as to have an approach leading up to the front of this building. But to have an entrance to one side and to spend a large sum in pulling down a building like the Russell block does not appeal to me in the slightest degree. It is quite evident that the Prime Minister has in mind for the future the widen* ing of Metcalfe street, but he does not say how far south of Wellington street the proposed widening o-f Metcalfe street is going to go; and I understand it is suggested that it is to be widened to from two or three times its present width. As I said before, if that is going to be done, the widening should go *t. least to Laurier avenue. If it does not go that far, how far is it intended that it should go?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To Lisgar
street, which is much further south.

That would make a much
more imposing entrance. That would be about seven blocks down Metcalfe street, and it can be figured out how much it would cost to widen Metcalfe street from two to three times its present width over that distance. Are there to be two entrances to the parliament buildings, one of them from where the Russell house is? Because that 'would not be a suitable entrance unless the post office is to be pulled down. Is the government going to pull down the post office and make that site into a park two or three hundred feet square? Then perhaps in four or five years are they going to undertake to widen Metcalfe street down to Lisgar street at a cost of goodness knows how many million dollars? We ought to make up our minds now what we are going to do. If it is the intention to miake an approach by 'widening Metcalfe street, we ought to save our money for that purpose. I want to register as firm and definite a protest as possible against the expenditure of this money to pull down a block in the heart of Ottawa, a block which is not essential to the improvement under contemplation, because the scheme will not be complete when the block is pulled down and the country will still be face to face with the Metcalfe street improvement outlined by the Prime Minister in his address this afternoon. I think we should go slow in the matter. I am quite in favour of making an annual expenditure in connection with improvements! in Ottawa on account of its being the capital city, but I do not think we should commit ourselves for a period of

Federal District Commission
thirty years. It might be all right to provide for a scheme covering a period of five years, but I want to register my protest against wild extravagance in connection with pulling down the Russell block and getting such a little return when we know that a great deal more has to be done in the future.

Could the Prime Minister inform the committee as to the cost of acquiring the property between Wellington street, Sparks street, Elgin street and the post office where the buildings have been demolished?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I have not the figures under my hand. I could give my hon. friend the price per square foot for that property, buildings and land, as purchased by the Department of Public Works. It amounts to $23.75.

I should like to say a word or two in support of the proposal made by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys). It is right in line with the suggestion I made last year that any further money we spend in beautifying Ottawa as the capital city of Canada should be spent directly in front of the main entrance of the parliament buildings. I should not like to state categorically how far south the widening of Metcalfe street should be carried out, but it would be much better for us to spend whatever money we can afford in widening Metcalfe street than in purchasing the old Russell block. My idea is that the government should expropriate the property on the west side of Metcalfe street so far as it is necessary to widen that street and as many blocks south as we can afford to go. Those buildings need not be demolished at the present time; they could be allowed to stand for the -next ten years if necessary, and in that time the rents coming from those buildings might largely cover the capital outlay we would incur. The view which the people are going to get of the parliament buildings from this area we are now purchasing will be largely a view of the east block, and many people coming to Ottawa will see the east -block from that angle and will think that is the parliament building. We should have a wide avenue leading directly from the main entrance of the parliament buildings into the heart of the city, and I can only regret that the government have not spent this money in purchasing the properties necessary to carry out that improvement instead of purchasing the Russell block. The -city of Ottawa is so badly in need of another hotel that it is rather a pity the government did not permit the former owners
of the Russell house property to put up a good hotel on that site and spend the money we are now using to acquire the Russell block in purchasing property which would enable us to provide a wide thoroughfare directly opposite the parliament buildings and leading down into the heart of the city.
Is it the intention of the government ultimately to expropriate the property between Slater street and Laurier avenue and Elgin street to extend the scheme up to Cartier square?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not in contemplation at the present time. I understand that within the area to which my hon. friend has just referred there is a block of buildings to the east of Elgin street between Laurier avenue and Queen street. A number of houses, a store and also a church come within the possibility of the enlargement of Elgin street which the city council have undertaken to carry out themselves and I understand they are doing that by a plan of deferred widening of the street.

With respect to the financial position I did not quite follow what the Prime Minister said. Clause 9 as it now stands is hardly the sort of clause we should enact. We admit that we have not the money with which to pay the interest. The $3,000,000 expenditure will cost roughly $135,000 a year when guaranteed by the Dominion, and there will be no provision for sinking fund, which for the sake of argument we will place at one per cent- That would make a total of roughly $165,000 or $170,000. Now of the $200,000 a year, it takes $150,000 for maintenance, and the rest for general work. I gathered from what the Prime Minister said that the government had no particular preference for any scheme of financing, but I am sure the minister will realize that if we guarantee $3,000,000, and the commission is to get the money and issue its securities, it is really, to use a word that was very much in vogue in this country at one time, camouflage, because the commission has no revenue with which to meet the interest, and, as provided by section 10 of the bill, the interest will be paid out of consolidated revenue. Why not make a direct appropriation for this purpose and provide that we will advance for the purpose of this work the sum of $3,000,000 out of consolidated revenue, instead of taking the securities of a commission which we have ourselves created, knowing that it will not meet any interest obligations, and that we ourselves must meet them, together with the sinking fund, as well as in the end pay the principal itself.

Federal District Commission

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What I wanted to say to my hon. friend was this. I understood that he had a preference for the principal sum being paid directly out of consolidated revenue. I hoped it might help to bring us all into agreement were I to give him the assurance that with respect to capital expenditures made immediately on the Russell house block, they would be made chargeable to consolidated revenue and be paid direct by the Minister of Finance. That would reduce considerably the total amount on capital expenditure to be met by securities to be issued by the commission. I think that might well remain optional with the [DOT]Minister of Finance. I am not sure that the minister might not conclude, when asked for the money for the purpose which these capital expenditures are intended to serve, that it would be better for him to meet that capital expenditure directly out of consolidated revenue. On the other hand, it might serve a useful purpose for the country to have the securities issued by the commission and guaranteed by the Minister of Finance, and distribute the payments over a series of years, seeing that those who will come after us will be benefiting by the expenditures in equal if not larger measure than we are, I think my hon. friend can rest assured that the government, if it is allowed that amount of latitude, will be most careful to take the course which is obviously in the public interest.

May I ask
the Prime Minister if the commission have
any other driveway scheme in mind outside of the one mentioned past the Russell house to Cartier square?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The commission has a plan that involves driveways through all parts of the city, and that scheme is being projected little by little. I think the greater part of it is now nearing completion, but I understand from the commission that the driveways were originally constructed, at a time prior to the U9e of the motor to anything like the extent it is being used to-day, and that most of the driveways will have to be widened and enlarged. A good deal of the expenditure will be in enlarging existing diveways.

The government own considerable property to the west of these buildings on Wellington street, and I was wondering if the commission had ever thought of running a driveway through that property, connecting with the Sherwood driveway, running around the rear of this building, then connecting up with the driveway to

Rockliffe. Such a driveway would avoid the tearing down of very valuable property; it would follow the river and get away from the traffic on the other streets, and would really make more of a scenic driveway than the other. I do not know whether it has been thought of at all, but it could be done for far less money, and would serve the purpose just as well.

In discussing this bill,
which is to vote funds for the beautification of this capital, I agree entirely with the hon. member for West Calgary that it would be in the interests of this country if the necessary moneys were to be provided out of consolidated revenue. First there is the $6,000,000, payable iat the rate of $200,000 a year, which is to be paid out of consolidated revenue. Then there is a further $3,000,000 for which the commission is to issue its own bonds or securities. They would issue bonds, say, at 5 per cent. They may get them for less, but we must reckon on a fair margin, and at 5 per cent we should actually be paying in principal and interest $7,500,000 for the use of $3,000,000 to beautify this city. I would like to see the capital beautified; I think it should be, but at the same time I do not want to impose unnecessary taxation on the people of this country. If you spread the $3,000,000 over the thirty years it would amount to $100,000 a year. Would it not be better to pass a statute to take this amount of $100,000 a year out of consolidated revenue fund for the thirty years so that we would get rid of paying the annual interest? I do not think sufficient consideration is paid in this house to the question of interest. It is the biggest tax we have to bear. It is the heaviest burden on the Minister of Finance in connection with the national debt and in the present case I think it would be much better to take $100,000 a year from the consolidated revenue fund, rather than to issue bonds for $3,000,000 on which we would be paying interest for thirty years, and which would eventually cost the people of this country $7,500,000 for the use of that $3,000,000.

Perhaps this is an appropriate point at which to repeat the question I put to the Prime Minister. It is the first question I have asked the Prime Minister or any member of the government since coming into this house, and as a matter of courtesy to the constituency which I represent I should like him to give me an answer. I understood the Prime Minister to say to this house, "Yes, we have spent so many millions,

Federal District Commission
but we have a real asset to show for it. We bought some town lots for you, and these town lots, as time goes by, will increase many times in value." The Prime Minister has said that this land cost $22 to $23 per square foot. At $23 per square foot it means, in the language of my county, over $1,000,000 per acre. Does the Prime Minister mean to say to the people of my county, "Yes, I have bought some town lots, but they are yours. They belong to the people of Canada. It is true I paid $1,000,000 an acre for -them, but if at any future time we decide to sell them for commercial purpose I will guarantee that you will get three or four or five or many more times the amount we paid for them." I would just like the Prime Minister to let me know if I misunderstood him, and if not, would he give me his reasons for thinking that this property is going to -become very valuable for commercial purposes in the years to come. If he can give me any good reason for thinking so, I would feel more like voting for this bill. If this is a foolish question, all right, say so, and let it go by, but I do not propose to have my first question in this house sidestepped.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that I have every desire to be courteous to him, and particularly to his constituency. I had no thought of evading any question of his, and indeed if I had assumed for a moment that he was asking me a concrete question I would have been very quick to reply to him. What I did say was that the amount of money which the government is expending at the present time is in the nature of an investment in land in the city of Ottawa. Personally I cannot imagine from the point of view of investment pure and simple a better investment that the government could make in real estate than to secure the best property in the city of Ottawa and hold it for the future of the nation. None of us knows what the demands on the city of Ottawa through the course of years are going to be. The day may come when an area in the centre of this city will be required by the government for a variety of purposes. The government of Canada will own that area. What will be its value then in relation to the small figure we are paying to-day? Not a small figure, it is true, when comparison is made with town lots in a small community, but relatively small with regard to the future. The parallel I drew was that at the time parliament hill was purchased there were undoubtedly many like my hon. friend who made comparisons between the
amount of money that was t-hen being paid for parliament hill and what was paid for town lots in the small communities from which they came.

But take Toronto, New
York and other cities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But those who purchased parliament hill made for Canada the best possible investment that could be made by that purchase. The government has no thought of selling town lots out of the area that it proposes to buy in this connection, but it is endeavouring to secure-

How is it a commercial
asset? It brings in no revenue in the meantime, it is simply a park for the unemployed to sleep in, and in the event of its being sold it must be disposed of for building purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not speak of the government speculating in real estate. I spoke about this as an investment-and an investment in more senses than one. I think if my hon. friend studies what has taken place in several large cities he will find that they have been saved from total destruction solely because of some open space or spaces which have prevented fire from extending further. Frequently I have thought of what the possibilities might be if this capital were to take fire, as the city opposite did on one occasion, and the fire should sweep through say from lower town to where the proposed park will be located. Such an open space in ' the heart of the city, from the point of view of insurance against a great disaster of that kind, is a factor which, having regard to its properties, the government might well take into account in connection with this proposal. I was regarding it solely as a national investment in speaking as I did.

I do not wish to be hypercritical; in fact I have not yet spoken of the proposal before the house, but is it not incorrect to suggest that the purchase of this property is an investment in any shape or form? An investment in the ordinary term is something upon which we get an immediate return, or, if not, we expect later on to have an opportunity of selling what we have purchased at an enhanced price. Of course the space outside these buildings forms a very fine setting, but, unless you use the w-ord in a sentimental sense, it was certainly never acquired as an investment. As the right hon. gentleman has suggested, it might be considered as an investment in the sense of affording fire protection, but it is decidedly

Federal District Commission 

not an investment from the standpoint of bringing any financial return, because we cannot imagine any circumstances under which we would sell that open space. Nor can I imagine any circumstances under which anyone could purchase from the government the area covered by this scheme. If we go through with the scheme it will be solely for the purpose of beautifying Ottawa, and not for any distinctly monetary return that it may bring us in the future. It has a sentimental value, if you will, or an open air or health value, anything of that sort, but certainly it has not any investment value, because by no stretch of the imagination will we ever think of selling it in town lots. The Prime Minister spoke of the open spaces in some of the European capitals. I well remember an open space to which he did not refer-Princes street in Edinburgh, one of the most beautiful streets in Europe. I think the open space between the Castle and Princes street has been preserved in that condition for centuries, and under no circumstances would Edinburgh think of selling that beautiful park, yet on the opposite side land is of the highest value because it is on the principal street of the city. So in this case I think it is wrong to create the impression that we are buying this property as an investment; it can be regarded as an investment only from a sentimental standpoint.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to delay matters but I would say to my hon. friend that the authority I had in mind in using the term seemed to me to be fairly, good. I have in my hand the report of the federal plan commission on a general plan for the cities of Ottawa and Hull, a commission appointed by the government of Sir Robert Borden. One of the phrases as I recollect, the commission somewhere uses with respect to the purchase of areas for parks and the like is that no better investment could be made. I cannot put my hand upon the passage, but the president of the commission was Sir Herbert Holt, and I think Sir Herbert knows a little about investments.

No one has more respect
for Sir Robert Borden than I have, but I should not like to accept every word that has been said by every commission appointed by him or by any other prime minister. Even if Sir Herbert Holt made use of the term, with all deference to his financial ability I would say that it does not properly express the idea that he probably had in his mind. Anyway, I am quite sure that all the investments of Sir Herbert Holt bring a much better

return in money than this investment will ever return to the Dominion.

I would point out to the Prime Minister that it is obvious, if you figure the outlay on an investment basis that the property will have to double' in value about every twelve or fourteen years in order to keep pace with the annual interest on the capital expenditure. Therefore I think it is a mistake to suggest that this is in any way an investment that will bring in any monetary return. The only justification for the outlay is from the standpoint of beautifying Ottawa. I should like to take this opportunity to say that unless the city council can find some better way of dealing with the filthy condition of the streets every spring-
Hear, hear.

-for a period of two months, they will have very little right to ask for further grants from this parliament. I know of no city possessing such remarkable natural beauty where the streets are allowed to get into such a filthy condition in the springtime as are the streeets of this city. I have observed this every year for the last eighteen years, and to my mind, and I say it advisedly, no reasonable effort is made to clean the streets. Their condition is not only inconvenient, it is exceedingly unhealthy. Inquire among your friends, and you find many of them are suffering from serious colds. They call it an epidemic of grippe, but it is nothing more than the result of the offscourings of winter's accumulation of filth.
I concur in the remarks of my hon. friend from Oshawa (Mr. Kaiser) that it is about time the capital city of the Dominion endeavoured to find a fairly decent water supply. The water in the city is not fit to bathe in, to say nothing of its use for drinking purposes. I have been looking for an opportunity to say this and I have said it in two minutes. And I mean it all. I could speak for half an hour just as strongly on the subject if it would do any good.

I want to make one or two observations in view of what the Prime Minister has said regarding driveways in the larger centres of population. It is true that in the larger centres there is a tendency to build driveways, but as a rule they are found on water frontages, such as lakes, to which they may be adjacent. In the suburban areas where residences and educational institutions are situated it is customary to

Federal District Commission
construct boulevards from eighty-six to 100 feet in width. I am opposed to this particular scheme because you are coming into the heart of the city and putting in a wedge, dividing upper town from lower town. It seems to me that business men and visitors who come to the city, desiring to do business in either section, will find it quite inconvenient traversing this area from Elgin street down to Sussex street below the Chateau every time they want to carry on a transaction; it will cause delay, and it will constitute a handicap. If you must have a driveway why not confine yourself to the outskirts of the city, as is done in Toronto? In Kingston the situation is very much the same as it is here. Going along King street, Kingston, if a driver wants to go to Queen's university he has to traverse almost a mile from the centre of the city through a park before he can reach that educational institution. This may be a means of beautifying the city, but from the point of view of the visitor who has business to transact it will be a great handicap when he discovers that the city fathers have seen fit to open in the heart of the city a park area, shutting-off one business section from another and one centre of educational institutions from some other. In my opinion we are making a mistake in dividing the city in this way, thus putting a wedge between two sections. It would be better business to build a boulevard of reasonable width up to Elgin street. Certainly I would not take this hotel away from the centre of the city. It would be more advisable in the interests of Ottawa to leave this commercial investment which the Prime Minister speaks about-and he did use the word "commercial"-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not use
that word.
He said "commercial investment."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I venture to say that if my hon. friend looks through Hansard he will not find the word "commercial". I used the word "investment" and possibly it was open to the broader construction given it by some hon. members; but I did not use the word "commercial".

I accept the Prime Minister's correction and I hope Hansard will do the same. I repeat, it would be better in the interests of those who visit the city on business if we had another first-class hotel on the site of the Russell house.

We have read in the press
that $1,125,000 has been paid for some property. Can anyone on the government side tell us from whom it has been bought, and what steps were taken to see that this is a fair price?

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Acquisition of property.

In subsection 2 of section
13 it is provided:
Any plan and description deposited under the provisions of the Expropriation Act may be signed by the chairman of the commission or by the secretary thereof.	.
Why not have it signed by the chairman or by one of the commissioners?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection to the change. I move that the subsection be amended by inserting the words "one of the commissioners" in place of "the secretary thereof".

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I say that in answering a question I gave a figure which I understood was the amount paid for the property between Elgin street and the post office, and Wellington street and Sparks street. I am advised that this is the figure at which the property was valued by the Public Works department, but the actual figure has not yet been finally determined, because there are still proceedings before the court in the matter of the expropriation of the properties.

In connection
with the whole of the property, or parcels of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say, but I am inclined to think it is the whole.

The right hon.
gentleman cannot give any information as to what that area will cost?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will give
further particulars when the bill comes up again. I move that the committe rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

It seems to me there are too many officials going over there. They are nearly all non-contestants.
PRIVILEGE-MR. NEILL On the orders of the day:

I
desire to rise to what I think is a question of privilege, and to correct a slight error. At page 2455 of yesterday's Hansard I find it recorded that the right hon. the Prime Minister, speaking in answer to an hon. gentleman opposite, said:
