Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 214, to provide for a loan to the Quebec harbour commissioners.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I assume that we .shall not discuss the bill on the second reading? There are some amendments we desire to offer, and I assume that that may be done in committee?
Yes.

I have not heard a single word which the leader of the

Quebec Harbour Commission
opposition has said. I do not like to ask him to repeat his remarks, but possibly, if they were of sufficient importance, he will have the courtesy to do so. May I ask you to see, Mr. Speaker, that order is preserved in the house?
Order.

I was suggesting to the
Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) that there were some amendments we desired to offer to this legislation, and that by going into committee at once, without discussing them at the moment, we would preserve our rights, and he said that was satisfactory.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-$8,500,000 may be loaned to harbour commissioners for terminal facilities.

With respect to this
bill and two similar bills that deal with the appropriation of public moneys to be expended through a harbour commission, I think it is quite apparent now from what we have heard during the last few days that the case made Iby the Minister of Justice with respect to Quebec harbour has been entirely unanswered. It is quite clear that if we are to treat that port as a national port, and it is the only deep-water national harbour that we have in Canada, this money should be directly voted to Quebec harbour, and be spent under the control and supervision of the government of Canada, and not otherwise. The Minister of Finance instructed the audit board to make a report with respect to the harbour commission at Quebec. That report was made and is now upon the pages of Hansard. Rightly or wrongly, the audit board was of the opinion that the harbour could not hope to earn interest upon this large expenditure, which is to be utilized in the manner indicated by the minister. That is now a matter of record.
Under those circumstances should this country play at financing and take securities that are promises by itself to pay to itself?- for that is all it means. The harbour commission securities are promises to pay by a body created by parliament, and those moneys are to be paid to the people of Canada; but the people of Canada are to find the money and the audit board has reported that the interest will not be earned. So what we are doing is taking promises to pay to ourselves that which we ourselves must pay. Therefore once more I appeal to the minister to make

this a direct appropriation to the harbour of Quebec. The harbour of Quebec has established its right to the money. The auditor's report establishes the fadt that the harbour commission has been expensively administering the affairs of the port, and that it cannot pay the interest. How then can we with any sense of financial consistency pass an act to authorize a body to borrow money which we know it can pay only iby money it gets from ourselves? I submit that the case made out by the Minister of Justice last week abundantly and clearly establishes that this harbour is entitled as of right to the expenditure of these moneys for the purpose of equipping it as the deep water port of this country over a period of seven months each year and perhaps longer.
I cannot possibly bring myself to vote to place in the hands of a commission, without the control df parliament over its operations and expenditures, the large sum of eight million dollars when we know that we ourselves must pay the money and the interest on it; and we will not pay 5 per cent interest, because if we borrow -the money ourselves, or pay it out of borrowed money, we will pay probably 4J per cent. If the minister persists in dealing with public moneys in that way, I can only say that there must be some reason to ibe given for it other than the necessities of the port; for certainly considerations of economy in financial operations and everything that makes for the proper conduct of public business will favour this being done by a direct appropriation of parliament. The harbour of Quebec has just as much right to the expenditure of these moneys as have other ports in various parts of the country to the moneys that are being expended on them. Having established that fact, we know that the harbour commission has been operating at a ratio of expense out df relation to that of any other harbour Commission in Canada; coupling that with the audit board's report that 'the harbour "will not earn interest on the advances, we should deal with this as a direct obligation by the people of Canada, and this year make an appropriation of whatever sum is necessary to discharge the initial obligations in connection with the undertaking. It may be that next year and the year after larger sums may be necessary to complete the work at Wolfe's cove and elsewhere in order to make .the harbour what it should be.
Once more I repeat, In respect of this and other harbours it is quite apparent that there should be a complete survey made by competent authorities to enable us to understand the situation in its entirety. On previous oe-
237}

Quebec Harbour Commission
casions the right hon. Prime Minister has referred to the importance of securing expert advice on our public undertakings, such as the beautification of the capital and the estuarial conditions at Fort Churchill and Port Nelson. Consequently when we come to deal with what so vitally affects the cost of moving grain, providing passenger 'facilities, and all that is involved in these harbour works, we should not lightly proceed without having the best advice obtainable. As we have not dealt with these matters on so large a scale as they have been undertaken by other countries, surely we are warranted in having that expert assistance and advice1 so essential to making this undertaking a success. If the minister is still of 'the opinion that, although he knows the situation is as reported' by the audit board', and persists in making advances to a commission, which amounts to nothing more than a promise tio pay ourselves certain money with interest, then I feel that he must surround his measures with safeguards which are not now provided.

I agree with the opinion
expressed by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) at the conclusion of his observations, that a survey of our ports should be made. I realize that the time has come when such a survey must be made and certain changes effected in the whole system of our harbour commissions.
As to making a direct advance to the port of Quebec, I would hestitate to ask for such a thing at the present time. It is true that the harbour of Quebec has not been in a position to meet its interest, but, as I explained and as the Minister of Justice and other hon. members who spoke on the matter explained, it is due, to a great extent at all events, to the fact that the port was not properly equipped and capable of giving to the harbour commissioners sufficient revenue to meet their obligations. They have always contended, as we ourselves contend, that when the port is provided with adequate equipment they will be in a position within a few years to pay, if not the whole, at least a part of the interest on the advance that we are making. Suppose we were to start with a direct advance to the ports of Quebec, St. John and Halifax; thereupon I am quite sure that Vancouver and Montreal would feel they were unfairly treated in that they were forced to collect dues sufficient to meet their obligations. In fact it would be unfair to place those ports in such a position, while the ports of Quebec, Halifax and St. John-which will be great ports before very long-were placed in the favourable position of not having to
pay any interest on moneys advanced. Af. present I cannot agree to act on my hon. friend's suggestion.
As to the payment of interest by the port of Quebec, I think it is important to remember that the major part of the eight million dollars which is to-day charged as interest in arrear is on loans that were made to the harbour long ago. In fact I think that the interest accruing on expenditures previous to. 1913, carried to January 1, 1928, amounts to. over six million dollars, while the interest accruing on expenditures since the organization of the commission in 1913 to January 1, 1928, is only three million dollars. By far the larger amount of the advances has been, made since 1913. Up to 1913 the expenditures totalled $5,307,106. On these expenditures we. are claiming from the harbour commission six million dollars interest; that is, we are claiming more in interest than the capital expenditures made up to 1913. These expenditures were made a long time ago to meet the requirements at that time, and I submit that it is not fair to charge to the present organization at Quebec an amount of $6,000,-. 000 of arrears in interest on an advance of $5,000,000 expended up to 1913. The real responsibility of the present harbour commission would be for the expenditures which have, been made since 1913. If we take into consideration the amounts loaned and the expenditures made the arrears and interest will be only $3,280,000. Against that there is, aa we have indicated already, the claim which the harbour commissioners are making against the Department of Immigration for the use of 40 per cent of the present facilities in the port of Quebec, and I think it is only fair that the commission's claim to a substantial; amount should be recognized and entertained by the government. If that claim were entertained it would wipe out the amount the. commission is supposed to owe to the government as arrears in interest.
I think the situation in the port of Quebec-has been to a large extent misunderstood. We have always spoken of that large amount of $8,000,000' of arrears in interest, but we have never taken into consideration the fact that these arrears have accumulated on expenditures amounting to $5,000,000 up to 1913. I repeat that the position of the harbour of Quebec which we should consider is the position as it has existed- since 1913. That is, only fair-
Mr. OAHAN; Why since 1913?

Because the harbour com-, mission of Quebec, as it exists at the present time, was so constituted in 1913. The body-

Quebec Harbour Commission
having charge of the harbour of Quebec before 1913 was not similar to the present organization. One might argue very properly, I think, that the expenditures which had been made in the port of Quebec up to 1913 ought to be considered in the same manner as the expenditures made by the Department of Public Works in all other harbours which are not controlled by any harbour commission.
"W hy should not the present expenditures be dealt with in the same way?

I see no objection to considering the present expenditures in the same light, but I contend that it would not be fair to single out two or three of our ports in Canada and allow them to go scot free in respect of interest on advances, while we make other ports which are just as important, from the standpoint of Canada as a whole-Montreal and Vancouver-earn money to reimburse the government for the advances they have received.
But there is no unfairness so long as there is no competition.

Even if there is no competition the situation is the same. You cannot compare Montreal with Vancouver. Vancouver can be compared with Halifax and St. John because it is an open port the year round; and it would have a good claim if it urged that in respect of expenditures which have been made in that port interest should not be paid. My hon. friend, with all his experience, realizes that once we open the door to an exception in reference to any one of these ports it will be a serious matter for the minister. He can readily understand what the life of a minister as well as of the government would be in view of the representations and requests that would come not only from the different harbour commissions but from all commercial and financial institutions; because we must remember that when a vote is before parliament, or when a request is made to the minister or to the government for an advance for St. John, Halifax, Montreal, Quebec or Vancouver, we not only have to deal with the particular harbour commission but we must face the representations and the very strong requests that come from these financial and commercial organizations in the localities affected. Boards of trade are always supporting representations made by commissions everywhere. I do not say that it would be wrong in principle for us to suggest that they should not be bound to pay interest, but it is unfair to single out and make an exception of three ports. I have promised to look into the affairs of these harbour com-[Mr. Cardin.3
missions during the recess and I propose, possibly at the next session, to introduce a new scheme to deal with the various harbour commissions in Canada. Then will be the proper time to place them on an equal footing, giving them the same powers and privileges. But, I submit, we should not impose upon one a handicap which will operate to the benefit of others.
In the circumstances I consider it only fair to the ports, and quite logical on the part of the government, to proceed this year along the same lines we have followed in the past. Of course it will be only a matter of procedure. Suppose we make an advance and have an amount placed in the estimates: so far as the money itself is concerned there will be no difference. Whether the money is advanced through the Department of Public Works or through my department by means of a special vote in the estimates, or whether it is advanced through the medium of particular legislation, there is no difference at all as regards the money. There is a difference in the mode of procedure; that may be true; but, I repeat, there is no difference whatever so far as the advance itself is concerned.
I think I had better take this opportunity of answering a few questions which were put to me by hon. gentlemen when we were dealing with the resolution. My hon. friend from Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) drew my attention to a certain figure I had given in 1925 when we discussed the advance of $5,000,000. He asked me what tonnage had passed through the port of Quebec and I replied, 594,614 tons. I am not sure whether I gave the exact amount, but at any rate I gave the figure 594,000. Possibly I was mistaken; according to the information which has been supplied me since, this represents only the imports. The exports for the year 1924 amounted to 206,285 tons. So far as the last year 1927, is concerned, the figures are not available; they have not yet been compiled. I can however give the figures for 1926. In 1926 the imports amounted to 865,611 tons and the exports 356,239 tons. If you compare the tonnage going through the port of Quebec in 1926 and 1922 respectively, you will find that the traffic has practically doubled. In 1922 the imports amounted to 499,620 tons while the exports only totalled 150,781 tons, and I may add that these figures do not include the lumber and timber exported through the port of Quebec. From year to year these figures show very conclusively that even with the incomplete facilities existing at that port the traffic has been growing very rapidly. As we have been told already, very serious complaints have been made by the people interested in shipping;

Quebec Harbour Commission
even this year representations were made by the Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited asking that greater facilities be provided. They requested an interview with the harbour commissioners to discuss the situation, and stated that if nothing could be done, if they could not get more than they have been able to obtain up to the present, they would have to refuse certain cargoes for the port of Quebec. I am informed that at present there are about twenty vessels in that port without accommodation, so that I believe we are absolutely justified in asking for this advance.

Is it not a
fact that the condition which the minister states now exists at Quebec, where a large number of vessels cannot be accommodated at once, is quite common in all Canadian ports? I have a distinct recollection of a similar situation which existed at Vancouver in spite of the excellent facilities to be found there, so that does not prove anything. Now, to go back to the other point the minister raised a moment ago, I would ask what facilities are lacking to have caused these complaints to come to him- in respect of the small volume of business now going through that port?

I have already indicated
the complaints; some of them have been received from the shipping federation. In 1925 they sent a long memorandum to the Prime Minister asking that the developments for which we are providing be proceeded with, stating that they were absolutely necessary. In addition to that we have had representations from the grain trade.

Were not
the complaints of the shipping federation particularly directed to the lack of berthing facilities? On the other hand, the minister has been discussing the lack of facilities for warehousing and taking care of the volume of goods going through that port.

I do not think it would be
profitable to build wharves with no sheds to take care of the cargoes; an ordinary wharf is not of much value without sheds and trackage facilities to handle the goods coming from the ships. To be complete, the port must have not only the proper docks but the sheds, the trackage and the other appliances necessary for the movement of cargoes over the wharves.

Would the
minister mind giving the committee any facts in his possession with regard to the unnecessary delay of ships through lack of facilities for loading goods?

I cannot give any particular
details in that regard; I must take the advice of those who know something about these things. I cannot discuss it with the shipping federation or the grain people, who are asking for an extension of the present elevator; they are supposed to know more than I do about these things; they are the experts dealing with the matter, and when they make representations to the department or to myself we must accept them. Surely I should not be expected to follow my own views or to adopt that spirit of opposition which may be in the minds of certain people.

I would not suggest, that the minister take that attitude, but I do think it would be common sense to accept the principle that in the case of any representations of that kind the minister should acquaint himself with the facts in connection therewith, thus placing himself in a position to supply the very moderate amount of information sought by the committee.

The representations we
have received appear to be reasonable, in the light of the information given us.
Just on that one important point, how many boats, if any, have been delayed while waiting to load goods as a result of the lack of facilities, and for how long have they been delayed?
Does my hon. friend refer to the past, or to the present year?

To the
present year.

I repeat that I cannot give any specific details with regard to any particular boat being delayed one day or two days. But I will place on record the letter from the Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited to the chairman of the Quebec harbour commission:
Dear Sir:-
It would appear that the berthage situation at Quebec this season is likely to he so acute as to probably result in our having to refuse to accept cargo for Quebec discharge and loading by our new fast freight boats, and as we are extremely loath to do this if the difficulties can be overcome, I would be very glad if you could make it convenient to grant an interview at an early date to Mr. W. M. Kirkpatrick, foreign freight traffic manager, and to the writer, in order that this question may be discussed.
Yours truly,
W. A. Wainwbight, Assistant to the Chairman.
I think I am bound to attach some degree of importance to representations of that character.

Quebec Harbour Commission

The minister quite properly does so; no one will blame him in the least, but he might also acquaint himself with the particular situation complained of. For example, I would like to ask him now what were the special cases referred to by the Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited? When did they anticipate the difficulties, and for what reason? Surely since the minister has had this interview with them he has acquainted himself with the details of the complaint.

No; they addressed themselves to the chairman of the Quebec harbour commission, who sent me these documents to support the requests of the commission. We desire this money to provide for four additional berths for vessels of the Canadian Pacific express type; two additional berths for large size ocean freight steamers and two berths for canal size steamers. So the money for which 'we are asking is to cover the expenditures necessary to provide for eight new berths which, according to representations made to me by persons who know something about it, are absolutely necessary. All the berths at present completed are occupied; the commission cannot provide any new berths if a company desires to increase its traffic, nor can they meet a situation such as that indicated by Mr. Wainwright. According to the representations made by the shipping companies and by the grain people, eight additional berths are required to place the port in a position to meet the present situation as well as conditions which probably will prevail within a very short time. I can hardly be requested to go into all the expert or technical details in regard to these matters. Suppose the expenditure were made through the Department of Public Works; the Minister of Public Works would have to rely on the reports he would receive from his resident engineers, supervised by the engineer in the department. We have to rely on somebody.

Well, it
may be gratifying to the taxpayers of Canada -it is not to me-to know that all that is required for the expenditure of amounts such as these are general statements by some shipping company or railway. The minister is not able to give us any details as to what losses have been sustained by the holding up of cargoes or vessels, but he says in general terms: I have had complaints from the railway and shipping companies, and therefore I am doing this.

I might give my hon.
friend a little of my own experience in the port of Quebec; which is the converging point of traffic on the river, both from the east and the west, as regards the Canada Steamship Lines. I travel extensively over that route every summer. I have seen boats coming up the river and down from Montreal to Quebec delayed an hour or an hour and a half and compelled to stay in the river until the day boat had sailed or until the Saguenay boat to Quebec had landed-all because the accommodation is so limited. Under present conditions it is impossible to provide accommodation for all the boats proceeding to or passing through that port during most of the summer. Some barge from the great lakes loaded with grain will occupy part of the berth ordinarily used by these boats; a boat will be coaling at another wharf, and as a result there is no room for either the ordinary passenger boats or the freight boats to dock. I have made inquiries of officials of the company in regard to the matter, and they have said: "We have been asking for the last five years for proper wharf accommodation, but we cannot get it. We are crowded and cramped; on the one side there is the pilot wharf"-I do not know what they call it- "and on the other side the accommodation is required by some other company. We need about three times the wharfage capacity we have at present, but we cannot get it because there is no room for it." So that I have personally had to experience the discomfort and inconvenience occasioned by this lack of proper accommodation in respect to freight as well as passenger traffic at the port of Quebec.

I endorse every word the leader of the opposition said this afternoon about dealing with these appropriations for Quebec. I think the time has come when it is necessary to inaugurate a policy in respect to these national ports. In respect to all large capital expenditures necessary for the development of these national ports, the appropriations should be made directly from the federal treasury and the expenditures made under the direction of or through a commission, but subject every year to review by this house. It is opportune at this time to consider a new policy, because my personal opinion is that in respect of the ports of St. John and Halifax, which are also national in their Character, the government, by making advances which are to be repaid by means of sinking funds, is placing upon them financial burdens which will actually in practice strangle their import and export trade. If we are to

Quebec Harbour Commission
develop a national policy of transportation we should make ingress and egress for passengers and freight at our Atlantic and Pacific ports, which come in competition with the ports of the United States on the eastern and western coasts, as inexpensive as possible. So far as we are dealing, therefore, with a national policy, we should consider the fact that the extension of these ports involves an expenditure wthieh is a burden for all of Canada. The government have recognized that principle in respect of ports on the Hudson bay. They must recognize it in respect of such a port as Quebec. We all know there is absolutely no possibility of taxing the trade of the port of Quebec sufficiently to repay to the government the capital expenditures by way of sinking fund while at the same time the port is paying annually the interest upon the debentures issued therefor. Hailbour commissions should be bodies authorized, under the supervision of the department, to supervise and manage the business of the port. A commission of business men could do much to bring to the ports of Quebec, St. John, or Halifax a larger measure of business than they now have. And the business of the port should be taxed to the extent necessary, and only to that extent, to carry on the operations of the port, and provide for the maintenance of such permanent harbour works as are constructed by direct appropriations from the treasury of Canada.
I do not wish to digress, but I think this is an appropriate occasion to lay emphasis on the importance of a change in respeict to harbour administration, a matter to which the leader of the opposition made some reference. The government are adopting a vicious policy in respect to the ports of St. John and Halifax. I do not pretend to know so much about the port of St. John, but I do look writh the greatest apprehension upon the application of that policy to the port of Halifax, which has been and I hope will contiue to be more in the future than in the past one of Canada's national ports. If the business of that port can be conducted so as to pay the operating expenses of the commission and a certain reasonable expenditure for maintenance from year to year, that is all that should be expected of that port. Otherwise the tax which you place upon the export and import trade will be so great as to make it impossible for Halifax or impracticable for St. John to compete with Boston, Portland, or New York. We must make them national ports; we must make them cheap ports for vessels to enter and clear, and we must conduct the business of those ports in as economical a manner as possible consistent with their efficient operation and sure development. Therefore I endorse most sincerely and heartily the suggestions made by the leader of the opposition. If we are to have national ports maintained in this country, the government must adopt that policy.
With respect to being unfair to other ports, the only two other ports to which such a policy might be deemed unfair, are the ports of Vancouver and Montreal. First, as regards Vancouver, I was sent some years ago by a large banking institution to make an investigation of the trade of the Pacific coast and I spent a considerable time upon that work. I came back with the profound conviction that, so far as Canada is concerned, a great volume of our trade, a volume that in a few years will, I believe, exceed the volume of our Atlantic trade, will certainly be going through the port of Vancouver. Vancouver may be doing very well at the present time and with the limited appropriations which have been made for the extension of that port it may offer a fair prospect of paying from year to year the interest on the capital expenditures which have so far been made. But if you are to make the port of Vancouver and the port of Prince Rupert further north, great national ports, this country must be prepared to make annually appropriations from the public treasury for the large capital expenditures which are necessary for their development, without looking for any return of interest thereon to the federal treasury. It will be quite sufficient if you leave to the commission of each port the exacting of the lessened port taxation to defray the ordinary expenses of operation and the expenses of maintaining in good repair the structures which have been built by direct appropriations from the treasury.
In regard to the port of Montreal I am not at the present time going into the larger aspect of the matter, namely, the development of the port in connection with the possible development of the St. Lawrence river. But the United States ports on the great lakes are the competitors of Montreal; the Hudson river will, I am sure, in the near future also become a competitor for Montreal's export trade, and if we are to develop Montreal's export trade in competition with United States ports, certainly large expenditures which are made in the port of Montreal must be made in the national interest, and justified from the point of view of the national interest, and this countiy must expect no return to its treasury of those principal sums appropriated but must be satisfied with a revenue from that port which will maintain its struc-

Quebec Harbour Commission
tures in good and efficient repair and ensure the operations of the port at such a low cost as will enable it to obtain and keep its business in competition with all rival ports lying to the south of the United States boundary. Therefore I think now is the opportune time, as the leader of the opposition has suggested, to inaugurate a new policy before you place upon the ports of St. John and Halifax a burden which cannot be borne by any prospective trade of those ports and which must prevent them from being developed as they should be in the national interest of the whole country.

On Wednesday last the minister quoted a letter which the harbour commissioners of Quebec had received from the central selling agency of the wheat pool. In case there might be any misunderstanding about that, I should like to read a telegram which I have just received from the man in charge of the central board representing the wheat pool. The telegram reads:
Smith's letter personal reply to General Tremblay. Quebec harbour improvements never discussed by provincial or central boards. Speaking personally believe pools in sympathy with general policy of harbour improvements that will increase shipments of Canadian grain through Canadian ports but naturally not in position to make definite recommendations to government.
(Signed) Geo. McIvor.

According to the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries a few minutes ago, exports and imports of freight through the port of Quebec in 1924 amounted to approximately 800.899 tons and in the year 1926 this had increased to 1,221,850 tons, or an increase of practically 50 per cent in two years. That is quite an increase in tonnage in a port the size of Quebec. Has the' minister any information as to the revenues in 1924 representing the tonnage of that year and also the revenues in 1926 representing the tonnage of that year?
According to the figures I have, the revenues of the harbour for 1924 were $568,727.77 and in 1926, $678,882.06.
That is an increase of about $110,000 for an increase of tonnage of 50 per cent. Can the minister explain why the revenues in 1926 have not increased in proportion to the increase in tonnage?
I must confess that I cannot give the details.
I take it that those are the gross revenues?

Yes.
TMr. Cahan.]

I should like to bring up again the question of the facilities handed over to' the commission in 1913 and also the liabilities with which the commission was charged. This afternoon the minister informed the committee that the facilities turned over to the commission in 1913 cost this country $5,307,106. He also stated at the same time that the interest charges on those facilities prior to the time that they were handed over to the commission amounted to approximately $6,000,000. Is that the exact statement the minister wished to convey to the committee?
Yes.

It is apparent to me that the Quebec harbour with this tremendous interest charge on the initial cost of the facilities has not had a fair show. I will admit that, and it seems to me that some remedy is required in that direction. I would like to see the government clear this situation up before we proceed much further with this bill, because if the commission remains with the same liabilities, in the event of it requiring a further appropriation as time goes on for the extension of the harbour facilities, the present situation will be only accentuated, and we shall be in no better position then to remedy that situation than we are to-day. So I would impress upon the minister the necessity of cleaning this matter up before we go much further. I am sure the committee would view such action on the part of the minister with sympathy, in order that we might give the commission the opportunity of starting from a sound basis; and once put on an efficient basis, if they are not successful, we shall know where to lay the blame. But as it is at the present time, we can hardly charge the harbour commission with any incompetency in view of the figures placed before the committee by the minister.
There is another point that I would bring to the attention of the committee, and which was discussed last week, and that is the question of the claims of the Quebec harbour commission against the various departments. I do not know whether the government have had the oportunity of going into this matter since the bill was last before the house, but I would ask the minister if he has had that opportunity. I should like to see Ottawa beautified; I should like to think we are now in the position to undertake that beautification; but in the course of my examination of my viewpoint in the matter, I find it difficult to come to the

conclusion that we are yet in a position where we may be able to afford the expenditure. I frankly do not think we are in a position to-day to do so. Had the Minister of Finance not been so gracious to the millionaires of Canada in his reductions in the income tax, there would have been a great deal stronger ground for the position now taken by the Prime Minister. I am going to find it very difficult to explain to my people and to the people throughout the country whom it is stated I represent, why I supported the expenditure of millions of money for the beautification of Ottawa while there are still thousands of people who in many cases are unable to maintain for themselves what is the ordinary standard of living in Canada. How am I to justify voting millions for beautifying Ottawa-and in the final analysis it is for vainglorious purposes; it is the beautifying of something for the satisfaction of our vanity-in the face of 8 per cent money for the farmers, and a wretched $20 a month pension for the aged and infirm who have toiled all their lives in an effort to build up the country? How am I to justify such a vote in the face of the fact that men are being jailed because they are unemployed? How am I to justify it in the face of the attitude of the government towards the Home Bank depositors, when all they hand the depositors is merely regrets? If I go to the fishermen of the maritime provinces and tell themj that I voted millions to beautify Ottawa, how can I justify my vote -when all they get is a royal commission to examine into their wretched condition? No other member can appreciate things of beauty more than I can or is more desirous of satisfying his desires for beauty and charm of surroundings. If I could bring down to Ottawa the tens of thousands of people scattered throughout this country who, because of social and commercial conditions that exist, are condemned to drab, drear lives of great toil and struggle with no hope of rising above a certain level of living and a certain environment; if I could take them down here for a holiday to enjoy this beautiful city and these things with which we propose to increase its beauty, I would feel easier in mind on the matter and a good deal freer to support the legislation.
In passing may I say that this prating about monuments to our wisdom, about the gratitude of posterity and the foresight and vision of statesmen, does not appeal to me, and the erection of monuments and parks utterly fails to satisfy my conception of the things that are really needed in the country at this mo-

Federal District Commission
ment. The time may come when all that may be justified, but it is certainly not now especially whilst thousands are struggling through life in Canada at wages which are below the standard of living. I undertook in connection with this matter to make an examination into some statistics, and I find that in spite of the fact that the select standing committee on industrial and international relations, a committee of this very house, in 1926 declared that the minimum standard of living in Canada would require an annual wage of 82,400, the great majority of the wage earners are receiving not much more than $1,000 a year. Here we have the situation where the great mass of toilers in Canada are living on one-half or less than half the wages which a committee of this house says is the minimum upon which a reasonable standard of existence can be maintained. Yet I am expected to go back to them and to justify a vote of millions for beautification while they struggle along through their unfortunate and frequently miserable lives in a condition relative to poverty.
I submit to the Prime Minister that it would be a far more worthy thing, a far more statesmanlike thing, if not all this sum but the larger portion of it were turned over to the relieving of poverty and misery and to a real attempt to solve the problem of unemployment, a problem which is growing more and more acute every year with the introduction of greater and more efficient machinery. The beautifying of Ottawa may be all very well for those whose salaries are now sufficient to guarantee them all the beauties -in life which they desire. It may be all very fine for the right hon. gentleman himself, and even for myself at the moment in a much humbler sphere of life, to satiate our appetites for beauty. But we have opportunities that other people in Canada will never have. If the Prime Minister would make an annual excursion for the people of Canada to come and see this city, there might be some reasonable excuse for this work. Let me say to him and to the leader of the opposition that while they were both in a measure correct with respect to the historical remembrance we have of Rome, Greece and even Babylon, my boyhood memory rather carries me to the achievements of the great generals, such as Hannibal, Alexander the Great and so on. If I read history in a less superficial manner than so many do. I find that with all that great display of military splendour, of wonderful monuments, architectural designs, parks and so forth, the most appalling slavery and destitution was the lot of the great masses of the people whether they were of Rome or Imperial Greece or Babylon, or of the unfortunate races who came under the sway of these empires. I think in doing what we are asked to do now we are simply preparing a vision for the eyes of those who are already wealthy enough to live in the Chateau Laurier, men who come here as lobbyists, as persuaders of government for the granting of special privileges. We are going to gratify their senses.
I want to say that in great measure our efforts may be wasted, because I can imagine many of these gentlemen who now reside in the Chateau Laurier would get a far greater thrill from the sight of a tax-free bond than from the sight of dawn on the bay of Naples or of a sunset in the Rocky Mountains, and yet we propose to spend millions in order that those who reside in the Chateau Laurier may gaze with admiration at about eleven in the forenoon on this beautiful park which the Prime Minister is asking us to establish-I will not say as a monument to has own memory particularly, but as a monument to our alleged statesmanship in this house. May I say in closing that he would have more worthily served the object he has in view if, instead of embalming in the industrial records of librairies those flowers of idealism that sprang to his mind in the past with reference to justice and humanity, and to which he gave utterance in his book Industry and Humanity, he had taken those flowers, now lying desiccated and flattened between the leaves of his book, out into the open and watered them by the application of practice. That would have been a far finer monument to his memory than ever this public park will be. If we turn our attention to solving the economic difficulties of our people we shall give posterity much greater occasion,to remember us than we shall by erecting a park to be gazed upon from the Chateau Laurier.
I am not opposing any attempt to beautify Ottawa, but I think that at this stage, in view of the condition of our finances, so long as we have over two billions of national debt and no reasonable method proposed for paying it off; so long as unemployment continues, with seventeen hundred men jailed in Winnipeg-not because they were not willing to work, but because there was no work for them to do last winter; and the chief of police of Winnipeg stated that in his opinion these men were, with one exception, of types as fine as had ever come to his notice-so long as these conditions continue there is no justification apparent to me at least for the voting of all these millions that are now being asked for. I submit that the Prime Minister would be well advised to reconsider the bill and to reduce the amount from $3,000,000 to $1,000-

Federal District Commission
000; or let us vote this thing year by year, if we are to vote it at all, instead of voting one lump sum at the present time. Let us proceed cautiously and reasonably, and not plunge into it as if we were as wealthy as Rome, Greece and Babylon together.
In passing, I agree entirely with the position taken by the hon. member for Macleod last night, that you are going to have a ridiculous left-handed view here under the plan proposed. Anyone walking out from the main entrance of the parliament building will not be able to gaze on a beautiful park. The view he will see will be the drab and miserable picture he sees to-day. There is no change contemplated along Wellington street, fronting the house. Only across to the left will there be a glimpse of the green sward and the flowers, as the proposal now stands.
Now that the Minister of Railways is in his seat, may I refer to the chief argument which he used. He said that this is such a small matter per capita that surely no reasonable excuse could be given for not voting the money. Identically the same argument could be applied to every vote that we have ever been asked to pass in this house. Taken by itself, the per capita taxation would be a very small item, as the result of any particular vote, but to use that as an argument why we should agree, with the condition in which our finances are, to vote this money is not good enough for me, and I intend to oppose this bill unless the Prime Minister can see his way to reduce the amount. I think he is asking for altogether too large a sum at this stage.
I hope that I have not hurt anyone's feelings. Let me simply reiterate before I take my seat that I would far rather support the Prime Minister in carrying into immediate practice those great ideals on behalf of humanity that he set forth in his book, Industry and Humanity, than fall in with this plan for the gratification of the vanity of those who expect posterity's gratitude-gratitude which can foe more justly anticipated if we seriously attack our great social and economic problems and by solving them bring charm, beauty and happiness to the people who toil.

I would like to get clear
in my mind what the difference is going to be if this project is going to be financed from the consolidated revenue fund. I would ask the mover of the amendment to the amendment kindly to explain to us what it is about, because we could not hear a word in this part of the chamber.

As the proposal stands
in section 2 of the bill, there was to be an annuity [DOT] of $200,000 payable for a period not 
exceeding thirty years from the 1st of April, 1928. That is the annuity; it has nothing to do with the $3,000,000, and that annuity is payable out of the consolidated revenue fund. The amendment of the right hon. the Prime Minister was to substitute fifteen for thirty years, and to that I moved an amendment that we do not bind the hands of parliament beyond the term of parliament, namely, five years.

I would ask the Prime Minister what is the interpretation which the government place upon this amended section 8. It says:
The minister is hereby authorized to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada to the commission the sum of two hundred thousand dollars a year for a period not exceeding . . . years.
Does that bind each succeeding Finance minister to pay that amount for the full term, or does it leave it to the discretion of each succeeding Finance minister whether he will pay it or not? It is "may," not "shall." What interpretation does the government place on this section?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If in the next
fifteen years there should be another Prime Minister he will be free to propose whatever he may think this house should give to the federal district commission.

That is not, I think, a
pertinent answer. I am dealing with the construction of the statute and with the practice. Where a Finance minister is authorized to pay for a term not exceeding, say, thirty years, does that bind the Finance minister to pay the amount each year? Is it not merely a permissive, and not an imperative, statute?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the
purpose of it is to give the commission the assurance that it will have, from year to year for the period of fifteen years, the money that will be required to maintain the improvements which it is making at the present time, and which it would not make unless it had that assurance. The commission is constructing driveways and parks now, and if it felt that it was not going to have the necessary sum to maintain these driveways and parks when completed, I do not think it would incur the original expenditure. This simply gives the assurance which will permit of a continuity and permanency of policy on the part of the commission.

I must confess that I read
the statute as permissive, and not as absolutely binding.

St. John Harbour Commission

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the
expectation would be that the Finance minister would give that amount to the commission for the period of time mentioned.

The suggestion has been
made that if bonds are going to be issued for this work, we should issue interest-free bonds. I would just like to remind the house that this is not an entirely new suggestion. It has been made not only by many eminent men in Great Britain, but by those who were associated with Heniry Ford in the large undertaking of the development of Mussle Shoals. It went so far there that a bill was introduced into congress and and secured considerable support. If we want this money in even amounts per year we could take it out of the consolidated revenue fund, but if we want more than $100,000 per year for the first few years, and at the same time want to extend the capitalization over a number of years, this is the way it could be done. Therefore I take pleasure in supporting the suggestion of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine).
Amendment to the amendment (Mr. Bennett) negatived.
Amendment (Mr. Mackenzie King) agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES

speechtext:
Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of bill No. 216 to provide for a loan to the St. John harbour commissioners.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Will the minister give the same undertaking with respect to St. John harbour that he has given with respect to Quebec harbour?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Absolutely.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
May I point out, Mr. Chairman, in order that there may be no misapprehension, that we think these moneys should not be raised by loan through harbour commissioners. In support of this view -I did not have it beside me the other day -I read from the Duncan report these words:
We are satisfied that neither at Halifax nor at St. John-although developments at St. John have been more extensive than at Halifax-is it possible, in present circumstances, to secure
adequate port development. We recommend that, in respect of each of these two harbours, the federal government should establish a statutory harbour commission, whose business it would be to see that the port facilities are developed on such a scale as will gradually-* but by no means slowly-create channels through which trade can expand both winter and summer. The development of a port is as much a matter of mechanical and technical equipment, business organization and practical administration, as is the development of any extensive manufacturing or industrial business.
We believe it is in the public interest of Canada, and in the interest of the future growth and expansion of its activities, that its Atlantic ports should be developed, just as it has been that its railways and canals should be developed-though development of these has naturally come first. We believe also from the evidence we have had that, under existing conditions of proprietorship at these ports, there will neither be inducement enough, nor impetus enough, to create really great ports, since for some time, at all events, it will be necessary to create facilities even ahead of expansion of trade. All that the Fathers of Confederation said about the importance to Canada of outlets and inlets on the Atlantic ocean open all the year round is as true to-day as it was then (and is indeed, from a commercial point of view, more immediately true now than then), and. in respect to ports-as well as in respect to the railways-the experience of the late war is fresh enough in mind to illustrate one phase of the national viewpoint and national necessity.
The words I particularly direct attention to are those that make it clear, as I submitted the other day, that the purpose and intention of the report was that the ports of Halifax and St. John should be developed by public moneys as national ports, because it is stated that they "should be developed, just as it has been that its-Canada's-railways and canals should be developed," namely, by the direct expenditure of public moneys. There is not a canal in Canada thus otherwise developed.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Our railways.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Our railways, publicly
owned, have been built largely by public moneys or guarantees of public moneys.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Guarantees.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Sir Andrew Rae Duncan said they should be treated as our railways and canals were treated, using those words in their generic sense. Evidently the Intercolonial railway was in his mind-a railway built by the people of Canada through the direct appropriation of their moneys for that purpose. This port will never be a national port in the sense in which the maritime commission meant it if you are merely to borrow money' through commissions for the purpose of extending it in the manner indicated. For let me point out that we have three illustra-

St. John Harbour Commission
tions here of what we may expect. Quebec wants eight million dollars for its harbour. The audit board said that the harbour commission cannot possibly make that profit annually on their operations. Halifax wants only $500,(XX); the interest on which is $25,000 per annum. The interest on the St. John loan will be $250,000 per annum.
Now, Halifax is a magnificent terminal. That terminal was bought by the direct application of public moneys to the harbour without any harbour commission, so that Halifax now requires only half a million dollars. St. John requires $5,000,000, which will place its harbour at a very great disadvantage with respect to the other ports on the Atlantic seaboard if tolls are to be imposed to meet the annual interest. Therefore it is my submission that the Duncan report contemplated with respect to the development of national ports at St. John and Halifax that public moneys should be directly applied for that purpose through the statutory commission operating in the administration and management of the port. The maritime commission were very careful to add one word more in respect to that:
We had. at our request, a private session with the Montreal harbour commission and, by hearing from them the steps they took to survey and stimulate production in their immediate territory as well as wider afield, we are confirmed in our view as to what harbour commissions (constituted of business and experienced persons) at Halifax and St. John could do in stimulating the trade of the maritime provinces.
It is those observations which I had in mind the other day, but not having the report under my hand I was not able to refer to them beyond my memory. I cannot think that we are doing our duty by the ports of Halifax and St. John if we merely create harbour commissions under the conditions of the existing Harbour Commissions Act, and ask those bodies to issue securities at 5 per cent per annum and expect them to pay either the principal or the interest. We should make an appropriation of such money' from year to year as is required for the purpose of developing those harbours, and it should be a charge upon the revenues of the Canadian people. We should not leave it to the defaults of the local body as happened in Quebec, because low tolls will have to be imopsed to make St. John harbour a success. For instance, how can St. John compete with Halifax if Halifax requires only $500,000 and St. John $5,000,000? How can you ask Halifax to impose tolls to raise $25,000 a year only and ask St. John to impose tolls to raise $250,000 a year?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The $500,000 is for one year, and the $5,000,000 for three.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Quite so, and that is all asked for at the moment. The interest required in one instance is $25,000-

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The $250,000 is spread
over three years.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The interest taken out of the $5,000,000 leaves that much less to be spent in the harbour of St. John.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: It is a three-year program.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Yes, and they have asked for $10,000,000. Now, if we are to Start in this way with these harbours we are mot doing our duty by the provinces, as indicated by that report, which sets out just what was contemplated. In ports such as Hamburg and London the tolls are kept down to the lowest possible level by reason of competition with other ports. But we are now imposing on these ports by this legislation the necessity of charging, for the use of the harbours, tolls that will have to be high enough to pay the interest on these moneys. The result will be that the port will lose the traffic, which will go through Portland, Boston and other ports. These moneys should be an expenditure by the Canadian people in consequence of estimates brought in and submitted to the house by the minister in order that we may be able from year to year to make our contribution to -the development of our ports until they shall have mat, in every possible sense, the requirements of the trade of Canada. It was for that reason t-hit I suggested to the minister that an- expert report be made with respect to Quebec. At any rate I desire to go on record, as positively -and distinctly as I -can, as being convinced that this proposal is not what is contemplated by the report, and never can make for the development of national ports. The ports must not be obliged to pay interest on the money we put into their development, and it ought not to be through harbour commissions that moneys are made available for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am sure that the citizens of the different -cities whose harbours we are now proposing to improve will look with some favour on- the attitude, which my hon. friend takes to-day. I may have misinterpreted the sentiment of hon. gentlemen opposite as expressed a few days ago when we were discussing the port -of Quebec. As I recall it, we spent the greater part of two days on that debate, every bon. member saying that Quebec was a fine port. But every hon. gentleman apposite made speeches and came out straight against any money being voted to the port of Quebec.

St. John Harbour Commission

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Name anyone who did so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
No, I will not name anyone.
I am in the judgment of tlhe house, and I may have misinterpreted hon. gentlemen opposite. It occurred to me early to-day, particularly when my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) was speaking, that hon. gentlemen opposite had developed a new policy in this regard. From the economy which they advocated last week they have jumped to the extravagance which we notice this week. They all want to dip into the public treasury, saying, at least by implication, that they are in favour of contributing money to the development of these ports without charging interest. That is a very popular policy with the people in the places where you are spending the money, but it is not so popular with the taxpayers.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Who will pay the interest in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: This is not a new policy my hon. friends are introducing to-day; it is a policy that has prevailed in this country for some time. We have spent millions, through the Public Works and other departments, in the port of St. John, and millions in the port of Halifax; and we gather from the information now before us that the work is not yet perfect and that they are coming back for more money. With that part of my hon. friend's observations-I am not sure that I understood him rightly-

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I take exception
to the remark that the government has spent millions in Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I take most decided exception to that statement. The expenditure was made as part and parcel of the railway system of the country and not specifically for the development of the port.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: My reading-

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I may add this:
In my judgment you might just as well say that the money spent in Moncton in connection with the railway, or the money spent in Truro or anywhere else on the railways, is spent by the government for the development of those places. The money spent in Halifax was spent in order to enable the railways to handle the traffic of their, roads. You might just as well argue that a clock without a pendulum is complete. A railway without terminals is not complete.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am not quarrelling with
the statement that harbour development is necessary, but I say that we have spent that money under departments of government and it has not been very satisfactory. In the first place the location of the harbour at Halifax has not been satisfactory, according to shippers and the citizens themselves. And I am told that the same thing applies to St. John. Now, coming back to the observations of my hon. friend, as to having a commission to look after all ports: I am inclined to that point of view. I should be willing perhaps to go even further than my hon. friend and further than my colleague the Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin). I think that all ports on the Atlantic-and maybe on the Pacific-should be put under one management and that they should all share in the receipts as well as the expenditures *with a view to developing good ports. I may say that I am not quite satisfied even with this legislation. But my hon. friend wants to dip into the public treasury and take out the whole amount. Now, my experience has been that if you have a commission responsible for the interest on the money that goes into the port, you will get a better administration, because they will take care of the interest. But when the money is spent at Ottawa the interest charges are forgotten; no one worries about the interest except the Department of Finance who have to provide it. I say to my hon. friend therefore that his party has made a wide jump from last week, when it preached economy, to this week, when it is preaching a doctrine which looks to me like extravagance.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am sorry the minister
should have made that last observation. It is in the interests of economy that we have been tiying all afternoon to strengthen the Quebec act. It is because the audit board, named by him, went there and made a report, which I read to the house this afternoon, that we have been endeavouring to prevent a recurrence of the condition that has prevailed in that port. It is our desire to have the spread between gross expenditures and revenues reduced from the amount reported by the board, and to have the accounts, the contracts and the expenditures sent to the public accounts committee for investigation. And the minister has been good enough to say that this will be done. It is because we believe in national economy rather than national extravagance that we urge that the ports of St. John and Halifax be nationalized by the expenditure of public money under proper control.

St. John Harbour Commission

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
We have had -that all these
years.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION I.OAN OF $5,000,000 FOB TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The people of St. John owned their own port without a commission, and it is only since 1913 that there has been a commission in Quebec. In Halifax there has never been a commission, and the Dominion government built there, in connection with the railway terminals, wharves Which are a part of the railway expenditures, as the Minister of Finance knows. The minister urges economy:	that was the very point I endeavoured to make when I said that we should vote a given sum per annum instead of $8,000,000 to the port of Quebec in the first instance, $5,000,000 to St. John, and some other sum to Halifax. Let this parliament vote the sums of money required for this year, that the accounts may be in the hands of the Receiver General, that the Auditor General may review them and that we may have a parliamentary inquiry to ascertain whether or not for each dollar of the money spent we have received one hundred cents in value. We urged this last week; we have urged it this week and we will urge it next week. We protest against the extravagance with which public moneys are being squandered in 'this country, and in the light of the expenditures which are being sanctioned it ill becomes the minister to say that because we are endeavouring to tighten up the safeguards and to protect the public exchequer we are therefore endeavouring to be extravagant with the public money. He had to admit the other day that there was no likelihood of interest being paid on the money lent to the Quebec harbour commission; I read the words of the audit board this afternoon, and if you impose tolls and charges for dock services in Halifax and St. John for the purpose of making a return on the money invested at from one-half per cent to one per cent more than it costs this country for money, you cannot hope to have those ports compete with other Atlantic seaboard ports. It is because of the Duncan report which has been adopted by this house and because of the desirability of making these ports free as far as it is possible to make ports free by reducing port and dock charges to a minimum that we urge that the government, which means the people of this country, should take over directly the administration of the ports through a statutory commission. The Duncan report did not specify a commission such as then existed at any given port. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries referred to what was said with respect to Montreal. The Duncan commission studied the operations of the port of Montreal, but as the minister has said, Montreal and Vancouver are exceptional

ports. The commission urged the appointment of a statutory commission composed of experienced men. After investigating the situation, the commission recommended that these harbour boards be composed of experienced business men. It was because of ' that very recommendation that I directed attention the other day to that question in regard to these two ports.
Extravagance as against economy is what the minister is now embarking upon, and since the government now are voting a three-year program here, a sixteen-year program there and a five-year program somewhere else, the Minister of Finance cannot hope to have that economy of control which comes from voting money from year to year to meet the necessities of a given situation, after he had received the report of an expert to ascertain what should be done to make out a rounded program. Parliament exists for that purpose, and when we hand money over to another body parliament divests itself of its control unless it is specifically preserved. If we spend two or three days or two or three weeks on this matter and at the end secure recognition of the fact that this house shall have control over expenditure of public money, then the two or three days or weeks will be well spent. That is all I have to say to the Minister of Finance, and in our efforts to assist him in the conduct of his affairs in an economical and inextravagant manner we should receive his assistance and support instead of being misrepresented as to what we have said.
Progress reported.
